utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case IT-96-21-A, the Prosecutor versus Delalic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The late start was a result of some problems out of the unit, and the commander out there has apologised for the delay. Mr. Farrell, there was a matter which we discussed briefly yesterday. That was the confidentiality of the motion which the Prosecution filed and of course of the order that we made on it. Do I correctly understand you that you no longer seek confidentiality for that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It's not a great concern of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It was not a great concern to the Prosecution. It was done as a matter of caution. So at this point in time we don't have grave concerns in that regard, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, I think we'll make an order lifting the confidentiality of the motion and of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, who is going to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In terms of the order of this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Ackerman, if I understand, had about five or ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, I am sorry, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, that's right. We did prevent you from going on. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I couldn't help but notice that we managed yesterday apparently to bore the public gallery absolutely to death, since they've not returned today. I hope we didn't do the same thing to all of you. I have two matters left to discuss, and I think I'll be quite brief with regard to both of them. The first has to do with the Prosecution's contention that the Trial Court erred in not permitting them to put on rebuttal evidence or to put on that same evidence by reopening their case. The Trial Chamber with regard to that issue basically found that the Prosecution had not exercised due diligence in acquiring that material at the appropriate time and presenting it to the Trial Chamber at an appropriate time. As you all know, the Tadic case, that issue was discussed, that issue of due diligence, and in the Tadic case it was found that the requirement of due diligence is not satisfied where there is insufficient attempt to invoke such coercive measures as were at the disposal of the International Tribunal, and that was a position urged by the Prosecution in that case. The other thing that I want to mention very briefly with regard to those materials. Very much like the materials that were presented to you yesterday with regard to the Prosecutor's most recent motion, the materials that the Prosecutor sought to introduce by way of rebuttal or reopening of the case were presented to the Trial Chamber, so the Trial Chamber was privy to the content of those materials. The Trial Chamber was in a, of course, very unique position to consider the force of those materials and whether it would have made any difference to their consideration of the case whether witnesses were brought to prove up the reliability of those documents. The Celebici case had at that point gone on for many, many months, beyond what anybody had predicted, and the Trial Chamber basically concluded that the documents were simply cumulative of information that had already been brought to them. So I think that this ground should be rejected by the Appeals Chamber. In our brief you will find a very detailed account regarding the factual background and our argument regarding that issue. I will now move to the issue of count 48 and the Prosecution's contention that the trial court erred by not convicting Mr. Delalic [Realtime transcript read in error "Delic"] of illegal confinement pursuant to count 48 as an aider and abetter. As I point out in some detail in the brief, it is our contention in that Mr. Delalic [Realtime transcript read in error "Delic"] was not charged in the indictment as an aider and abetter in count 48. If you look at count 48, what it did does is charge him only under Article 2(g). There is no mention in count 48 of either 7(1) or 7(3). I point out in the brief a number of indictments, both prior to and subsequent to--

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. There seems to be a little problem with the transcript. It's just been pointed out to me that the transcript keeps saying "Delic" when it should be saying "Delalic." If that could be just corrected in the final version. Your Honour, it's not the first time this kind of thing has happened, and we just watch for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I can't imagine what Mr. Ackerman's interest in Mr. Delic's situation would be, and the fact that he's speaking would make it fairly clear, I think, but I'm sure the typist will see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have outlined for the Appeals Chamber a number other indictments in this Tribunal regarding charges of aiding and abetting, and all of those indictments where the Prosecutor intended to charge someone with aiding and abetting, they did so specifically, if not in direct language, at least by reference to Article 7(1). The Delalic indictment only makes reference to Article 2(G). It is clear, however, from reading Article 48, that it's the intention of the Prosecutor to charge him under 7(3) as a superior because that's contained within the language of the charge itself. Even though 7(3) is not cited as a basis for it, it's clear that's what the intent was. But there's no indication from reading Count 48 of the indictment that he's being charged as an aider and abettor for direct responsibility for the illegal confinement of civilians at the Celebici camp. Even if it could be determined that he was so charged, the evidence would not support a conviction of aiding and abetting. As is pointed out in the brief, the Furundzija Trial Court did a significantly long analysis of what the elements are of aiding and abetting and concluded that the accused has to have committed acts that had a substantial effect on the perpetration of the crime and knew that these acts assisted in the commission of the offence. The Tadic appeal decision, at paragraph 229, has since adopted that reasoning. Also since that time and since the Prosecutor's brief was filed, the Prosecutor has, in fact, conceded the point where in the Kvocka case, in the Prosecution's submission of the updated version of the pre-trial brief, the Prosecutor concluded that in respect of aiders and abettors, it's required to prove that the accused committed acts that had a substantial effect on the perpetration of the crime and knew that these acts assisted the commission of the offence, which is different from the contentions made in the brief. We suggest, therefore, that this issue has been firmly settled in the Tribunal and that there's no reason for this Appeals Chamber to revisit that issue. I want to conclude by speaking briefly about what appears to me to be a glaring inconsistency in the Trial Chamber's judgement regarding the status of the persons confined in Celebici. For Count 48 purposes and others, they were deemed by the Trial Chamber to be civilians illegally held and illegally confined. The Prosecutor has admitted, in their pre-trial brief in the Celebici case and even in their arguments here yesterday, that if civilians confined are a security risk to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then the confinement is not illegal. On the other hand, the Trial Chamber, to bring the Celebici detainees within the protection of the Geneva Convention and define them as protected persons found that: "The Bosnian Serbs had clearly expressed their wish not to be nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina by proclaiming a constitution rendering them part of Yugoslavia and engaging in this armed conflict in order to achieve that aim." In other words, to make them protected persons, the Trial Chamber concluded that they were basically rebels who were opposing the lawful government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I submit to you that they can't be both. They can either be innocent, illegally detained civilians or they can be rebels taking up arms against their legitimate government, but they can't be both. It seems that these positions are clearly inconsistent and that the Trial Chamber essentially arrived at a result which was based upon those inconsistencies, on the one hand defining them as persons who had rejected the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, therefore, making themselves security risks, even if they were not in the process of taking up arms if they were part of this new constitution and in part of this process of engaging in armed conflict against their legitimate government, even if they were available to provide information to enemy forces, available to act as spies, subversive, or anything like that, they clearly were, according to the Trial Chamber, had demonstrated their allegiance to a foreign power, and I think under any analysis, it was appropriate to detain them under those conditions. So that inconsistency, it seems to me, is difficult to resolve. That concludes my argument regarding Count 48, and I think all of the matters that were on my plate under group 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this question in relation to the last point: If all they were doing was proclaiming themselves independent and part of what became Republika Srpska, that justified their detention, did it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If all they did was say, "Gee, I think it's a good idea to have an independent Republika Srpska or make ourselves part of Yugoslavia," no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If they had signed a document saying they regard themselves as being independent, does that justify detention?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think -- the problem is, Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's job to prove these things beyond a reasonable doubt, and the Prosecution offered no proof whatsoever. Each of the witnesses who came, the Prosecution never asked them what their status was regarding the uprising against the legitimate government, and it's the Prosecution's job to prove these things beyond a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Who is starting from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. I just wanted to indicate that Mr. Fenrick proposed first to reply to the submissions that have been made on the legal aspects of superior responsibility. I would then propose to reply to Mr. Ackerman and to Mr. Moran on the factual aspects and to respond to Mr. Kuzmanovic in relation to Mr. Mucic's ground of appeal relating to superior authority. If my understanding is correct, Mr. Kuzmanovic would then reply to us after our response. There were just a couple of housekeeping matters which I thought might be convenient to get out of the way here and now before we proceed. The first matter is that Mr. Fenrick is here as part of the Prosecution team in relation to the command responsibility issues, and with the leave of the Court, we would request that he be excused at the end of this hearing on group 1 issues. The second matter relates to the Spanish translations of certain documents that have been agreed to between the Prosecution and counsel for Mr. Landzo. Yesterday, the translations of the Spanish press articles were provided by my colleague Mr. Murphy. I did want to indicate that the translation that was provided is mutually agreed to by the Prosecution and counsel for Mr. Landzo. As also was indicated yesterday, we now have translations of the presidential decrees that have been referred to in documents filed before that have been published in the Official Gazette of Costa Rica, and I would now like to provide those translations to the Court as well. I have one copy. If I could provide that to the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And this is the subject of an application for them to be admitted, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I think it's by agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That they will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: We have an agreement filed already that the Official Gazette is a publication, the Official Gazette. The translation that's now being provided is mutually agreed between the parties. What I would just indicate in relation to that translation, because of the time limits that we were acting under, it was not possible for us to translate the entirety of both decrees, so we have provided with the translation a copy of the original in which we have highlighted the relevant parts of the decrees that have been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you only the one copy for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: We can provide more copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It might be an idea, and someone can mark out the blue outlining too in the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The other two things simply to mention in relation to this translation, we notice that because of the quality of the original, the translators weren't able to read some of the text. You'll see question marks have been inserted where it wasn't legible. We think those portions make no material difference. We think the translation's quite clear as to what the purport and the content of the document is, and we notice that there does happen to be one typographical error which, unfortunately, is in Elizabeth Odio-Benito's name, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could indicate. I have had the advantage of seeing these translations. They are acceptable. The one typographical error simply accredits the Judge with a more Nordic background than we would have suspected, but, Your Honour, Mr. Staker is entirely right. There is nothing relevant to the appeal in the passages which the translator was unable to read and we're perfectly happy with those translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Fenrick would begin presenting the submissions in reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honours, in our reply we would like to begin by emphasising that at no time does the Prosecution submit that the requirement for a superior/subordinate relationship is not an essential element of the doctrine of command responsibility. Our submission has to do with the scope of the superior/subordinate relationship, not with whether or not it is a legal requirement. If I may, since my learned colleague yesterday quoted from an article which I had written, if I may read part of the following paragraph. The particular article is one called "Some International Law Problems Related to Prosecutions Before the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia." It was published in the fall 1995 issue of the Duke Journal of Comparative and International Law. And the paragraph following the one that was cited states, in part: "Despite the problem of extrapolating an analogous doctrine of command responsibility for civilian leaders, the Tokyo decision can be used as a guide for establishing that civilian leaders can be held culpable for certain acts of subordinates."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading, for the interpreter's benefit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I apologise. "The Tokyo decision provides support for the following propositions." And then there are a list of propositions, the fourth of which is: "Political and bureaucratic leaders may be held responsible for the acts of subordinates when the leaders have a duty established either directly, by international law, or indirectly, by domestic law or practice, to ensure that their subordinates comply with the law and the leaders fail to fulfill that duty." In connection with the superior/subordinate relationship, Your Honours, we would submit once again that commanders or superiors can be of virtually any military rank. In a military context in particular, we can have a commander at the rank of corporal, we can have a commander at the rank of general. The rank is insignificant as long as it is, in fact, superior to the subordinates. Secondly, we would submit very clearly that a superior position can be rooted in de facto authority. In fact, what we would submit is an example of a lot of the points we would like to make is the Aleksovski case. Aleksovski is perhaps after a fashion an example of de facto authority. It's also an example of influence, because Mr. Aleksovski was a civilian who was appointed to be the warden of a prison. The prison staff consisted of military police. In a normal military hierarchical context, a civilian would not exercise any -- would not be in a direct chain of command over military police. Military police would be in a chain of command going up a strictly military hierarchy. But nevertheless, in the Aleksovski case, the Court held that in addition to the normal military chain of command, Mr. Aleksovski, perhaps by as a result of de facto authority or influence, exercised a degree of command authority over the guards at the prison camp. And indeed both the Appeals Chamber and the Trials Chamber went on to note that Mr. Aleksovski had no legal authority to punish the guards in the camp. The most that he could do was report infractions to military superiors and then the military superiors would be expected to take the disciplinary action. It is our submission that influence, as an aspect of the superior/subordinate relationship, is something which requires that the influence holder, or that particular kind of superior, exercises effective control over perpetrators in the sense that he or she has the material ability to prevent and punish; the powers of influence must be substantial, immediate, sufficiently related to the violations, and capable of permitting steps to be taken to prevent or punish the violation. We were asked yesterday for examples. We would suggest that examples would include Mr. Aleksovski, who's not in a direct chain of command; the numerous cases, particularly the high command and hostages cases arising out of the Second World War war crimes trials, where you had occupation zone commanders who were not in a direct chain of command, nevertheless being held responsible for an Article 7(3) type of command responsibility. There is also the military advisor, as referred to in paragraphs 3.26 to 3.28 of our brief, the initial appellant's brief. Concerning the knowledge standard, the meaning of "had reason to know," more specifically, we most certainly do agree with Mr. Moran's comment that the nullem crimen principle applies to forms of criminal participation as well as to the designation of offences. That being said, however, we would say that the assessment put forward in our brief and in the Blaskic trial decision provides a more accurate picture of the meaning of "had reason to know" than that provided in the Tadic appeal -- or excuse me -- in the Celebici trial decision. Indeed, if I might quote from the Blaskic trial decision, which in turn quotes the United States field manual, 27-10, on the law of land warfare, and this is a 1956 document. In paragraph 323, the quotation from the US army manual is: "The commander is responsible if he had actual knowledge, or should have had knowledge, through reports received by him or through other means, that troops or other persons subject to his control are about to commit or have committed a war crime and he fails to use the means at his disposal to ensure compliance with the law of war." With respect to Mr. Ackerman's observation that the Aleksovski judgement agrees with the Celebici trial decision concerning the meaning of "had reason to know," I could only suggest that the Court read paragraph 80 of that judgement, which was the one referred to by Mr. Ackerman, and I would suggest that it certainly does not agree with the Celebici judgement. It's quite ambiguous. It's simply not clear on what its version of the knowledge standard is. Concerning failure to punish, Mr. Moran referred to his experience with the American military system. It would be our submission that military justice systems do vary widely concerning who has a responsibility for punishment, and we would submit that if one looks at the commentaries, the ICRC commentaries to the additional protocols, that relatively authoritative source certainly indicates that the power to punish may be very limited in certain circumstances and may, in fact, be limited to a reporting obligation. And indeed in the Aleksovski decision, this Chamber accepted that Mr. Aleksovski could be held responsible on the basis of Article 7(3), when it was quite clear that he had no immediate power to punish the military police who were the prison guards, and all he could do in that case was to report. As one last observation, the Prosecution has submitted that there are three essential elements to the doctrine of command responsibility: the superior/subordinate relationship, the knowledge standard, and the failure to take necessary and appropriate measures to prevent or punish. There is no fourth criterion. The fourth criterion of causation to which Mr. Moran has suggested exists does not exist. That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, I'm just looking at the terms of the Article 7(3), which, after all, does give us our jurisdiction, whatever it may do about stating the law, and the knowledge factor, as you describe it, is if he knew or had reason to know. The words "had reason to know" would, of course, include "had knowledge of certain facts" from which he should have known. Are you asserting that "reason to know there" would also include "by reason of his command position and the duties which it entailed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, with the emphasis on the "and duties it entailed." As I said before, we're not suggesting that there is a strict liability standard, but we are suggesting that interpretation of that provision and interpretation of the doctrine of command responsibility requires that due regard be made to the duties that are imposed on a superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you say those duties are imposed by customary law and this picks it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would say it's imposed by the range of legal obligations which exist applicable to the particular individuals we are talking about. That would include customary law. It may, if treaty law is applicable in the circumstances, also include treaty law. It may, for that matter, also include domestic legal obligations, and, frankly, to go beyond that, it may, as a result of practice, be a de facto obligation, but all of these things can be taken into account in determining the extent of a duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fenrick, could you clarify something for me? If I have quoted you correctly about the superior authority [In English] measures to prevent or punish. [Interpretation] You talked about a fourth criterion. This criterion you called the criterion of causality. What I'm interested in is whether these three criterion are applicable to what you called "influence." I don't know how we would translate it. That is, exercise certain influence. It seems to me that this is a concept which is a little bit vague, but is this necessary if we are referring to these three criterion? There are persons who exercise influence and people who act under someone's influence. Does this only refer to the superior/subordinate relationship? If I understood you correctly, this person may not be a military person, does not make part of the chain of command. They have a de facto control and they de facto control their subordinates. So my question to you is: What does this concept of influence -- how does it relate to the three criteria which you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be the submission of the Prosecution that whenever the doctrine of command responsibility applies, all three of those criteria must be applicable. It may be that the duty to determine or to "establish" a system to report violations and the requirement to monitor that system may be very loosely interpreted, but there still must be more -- the person who is held responsible on the basis of Article 7(3) must be someone to whom one can legitimately impute all three of these responsibilities. If you do not perceive that, at any rate, a de facto duty to determine whether or not offences have been committed exists, then it would be our submission that the criteria for 7(3) are not met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have not answered my question on the influence. What is the significance of the concept of influence on all of this? Because at one point you mentioned persons who exercise influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It would be our submission that perhaps that influence is almost a form of de facto command. There has got to be -- it's a special form of de facto superiority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, if I may just come back a moment to the question that was earlier put by the Presiding Judge about knowledge. Just to be clear on your position, you mentioned that -- if I understood correctly, Article 7(3), has to be interpreted in the light of various sources, customary law, treaty law, national law. May I know exactly which is the place you give to the Additional Protocol, to Article 86? Because yesterday you mentioned that it's not part of customary law, it's not in accordance with customary law. May I know exactly which is the place you put it? Because one has to take into account that provision is a treaty, on the one hand, and on the other hand, it's a piece of practice that can be used to establish customary law as well, especially taking into account that it has been ratified by quite a large number of states. What would be your position exactly on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position would be that, first of all, separate and apart from the customary law status Additional Protocol 1, certainly Additional Protocol 1 was applicable to the conflict as a matter of treaty law. Going beyond that, our view would be: Depending on the scope of interpretation one gives to Additional Protocol 1 or, excuse me, to Articles 86 and 87, those Articles may be regarded as a partial codification of customary law or they may reflect virtually all of customary law. Our argument is that the proper interpretation of Protocol 1 is the interpretation found by the Blaskic Trial Chamber, which is more or less in line with the submission that we have been making concerning the knowledge standard. If, however, that interpretation of the meaning of Articles 86 and 87 is regarded as inaccurate and there is a preference for the interpretation given by the Trial Chamber in this case or at the trial level in this case, it would then be our submission that Articles 86 and 87 are not a complete codification of customary law concerning the knowledge standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: With regard to an issue raised yesterday, a very interesting one, by Mr. Ackerman, to which you seem to be more or less opposed, he sticks to the fact that the superior has to have a de jure authority, and in this de jure authority is inherent the duty to prevent or punish. Now, you try to maintain the fact that de facto authority is important. Without going into some type of hypothetical details, suppose in case there is some kind of contradiction between the de jure authority and the de facto authority, which one is your favourite?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: One would hope they would both coincide, Your Honour, but in the event that they do not, I think one would have to have regard to the full range of actual circumstances. For example -- or an example that I used yesterday was the Queen of England is probably the commander-in-chief of the British armed forces as a matter of strict law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's a very good example, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: But I would think de facto she certainly does not have that kind of authority, and in that case, I would think one would rely entirely on the de facto authority. On the other hand, if what we were talking about was a military commander in the field who clearly had a legal obligation to control his troops, I think we would have to have a very, very high burden indeed before one could ever say, "Ah, well, this general had a legal obligation to control his troops but it just wasn't practical in the circumstances." If I may refer, and I believe one of my learned colleagues did on one occasion to the Sabra and Shatila incident, which was the-- these were massacres in Palestinian refugee camps back in 1981 or 1982, and following those massacres, the Israelis established a commission, the Kahan Commission, to look into what had happened, and that commission certainly did not claim to have legal authority to establish legal norms, but it's certainly something which has been paid regard to since that point in time. And one of the points that was made in that report was that if you have a degree of control over troops who you know are going to commit offences, you then have an obligation not to put them into combat if you know that they are going to commit a substantial number of offences. You can't say, "Well, they were completely uncontrollable and I didn't have anybody else around so I used those troops, and they went off and committed a whole bunch of offences, and because I couldn't control them, I'm not responsible for them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your answer is quite satisfactory, Mr. Fenrick. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fenrick. You're free to leave whenever you wish, and thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. I have two points in reply to the factual aspects of the submissions put by Mr. Ackerman on behalf of Mr. Delalic relating to the unlawful confinement of civilians, count 48. The first was the issue of aiding and abetting which was raised. We submit this was fully covered in our briefs, particularly the Prosecution reply brief. At paragraph 4.15 and following, we deal with the point that aiding and abetting was validly charged in the indictment. And at paragraph 4.22 and following, we deal with the legal elements of aiding and abetting as a form of participation under Article 7(1).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you just indicate where in the indictment there is a general charge? Because looking at it, you haven't followed what has now become the somewhat imprecise practice of the Prosecution to just quoting Article 7(1). It's not referred to anywhere except in relation to Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: The argument is dealt with in our brief. Our main submission is that there is no -- there are no legal procedural forms of an indictment. There are general requirements that an indictment must meet. If an accused feels that the indictment doesn't meet those minimum requirements, it's possible to bring a preliminary motion seeking greater specificity. But as set out in our brief, we say that the way the indictment was worded, it makes it clear that there is first an allegation of participation and then there is an allegation of superior responsibility. And the word "participation," we submit -- I have a copy here of count 48. It begins, paragraph 36 of the indictment: "Between May and October... Zejnil Delalic, Zdravko Mucic, and Hazim Delic participated in the unlawful confinement of numerous civilians." The word "participated" doesn't appear in Article 7(1), but "participated" is a word which we submit is commonly used to refer generically to all forms of participation under Article 7(1).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That it's imprecision, you see. This is not the occasion to debate it, but really the Prosecution's pleading styles do need a little revision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: The pleading style has evolved over time as well, Your Honour. Our point is simply -- I think it is a matter of ordinary legal parlance that one would refer to the different modes of participation referred to in Article 7(1) as forms of participation", and if one says that one participated in a crime, that means that the person, by one of the various means specified in Article 7(1), is criminally liable under that provision. And then the wording of paragraph 36 goes on to allege superior responsibility. So basically it's Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) that are both alleged. The Prosecution -- the main thrust of the Prosecution argument in relation to that ground of appeal wasn't that the Trial Chamber applied the wrong legal test in relation to aiding and abetting in relation to Mr. Delalic; it was simply that it didn't apply it at all. I can refer the Chamber to paragraph 1144 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber reaches the ultimate conclusion that Mr. Delalic was not liable under count 48 because he was not in a position to affect the continuing detention of the detainees. And I made the argument yesterday in relation to Mr. Mucic that that is not an element of the crime of unlawful confinement of civilians, and we say the Trial Chamber simply failed to address its mind at all to the issue of aiding and abetting. The next point in reply in relation to count 48 was the issue of civilians as a security risk to the state. This also is dealt with, we submit, fully in our briefs, but I make the point again that merely because even if it can be said the Serb population generally had taken up arms against the government, this does not provide a justification for rounding up every single member of the Serb population. There is a difference between civilians who may present a security risk and those who do not. Mr. Ackerman said that the burden was on the Prosecution to prove that beyond a reasonable doubt. That is of course true, but that obligation is on the Prosecution before the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber made very express findings that the Prosecution had discharged that burden. There I would refer to paragraph 1134 of the Trial Chamber's judgement, where it said: "...the Trial Chamber is convinced that a significant number of civilians were detained in the Celebici prison-camp, although there existed no serious and legitimate reason to conclude that they seriously prejudiced the security of the detaining power." Now, the Trial Chamber made that factual finding on the basis of the evidence before it, and now before the Appeals Chamber the burden is on the appellant to show that that conclusion was so unreasonable that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached it, and our submission is that in this appeal that burden has not been discharged. If I then turn in reply to the submission of Mr. Moran, unless there are any further questions in relation to that, Your Honour. The submissions of Mr. Moran in relation to Mr. Mucic's -- sorry -- Mr. Delic's response to the Prosecution appeal. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Mr. Moran said that the fact that Mr. Delic was perceived by the detainees as the commander of the guards was absolutely irrelevant to anything, and he also said it made no difference that the guards called him "boss." In reply, we would simply concede that these two facts aren't necessarily of themselves conclusive, but we'd certainly say they're relevant and, depending on the evidence, may be of considerable significance. Mr. Moran said that the fact that Mr. Delic could give orders to the guards does not necessarily show that he was the commander, since he might have been exercising delegated authority like a chief of staff. Our reply is that even if it were the case that a direct chain of command is required, and we've presented submissions on that, it would still be open to the Trial Chamber to conclude from all of the evidence that Mr. Delic in the circumstances wasn't exercising that kind of authority but was exercising a form of direct command. That might be inferred from the evidence of the manner in which orders were given. And in that respect, we note that on the evidence, Mr. Delic was physically present amongst the guards, shouting at them and so forth, and we argue that on the evidence, the only reasonable inference is that he was exercising de facto the function of the commander of the guards. In relation to count 48, the unlawful confinement of civilians, Mr. Moran said there was no system in the world where prison staff make the decisions about who is detained and who is not, and that camp personnel can't be found -- or prison personnel can't be found liable if it turns out that the authority committing a person to prison has made a mistake. Our reply to that is that this is simply not true if the prison staff have actual knowledge that the detention is unlawful. And to give an example, suppose that a local corrupt police chief and several corrupt local police officers went out and simply dragged a person off the street in order to settle an old personal score, basically kidnapped them, took them around to the local prison and said to the commander, "Keep this person locked up here," and the prison commander knew all of the circumstances. We would submit that in those circumstances in any civilised system that the prison commander would be liable for the unlawful detention of the victim, and that if the prison commander gave an order to one of the prison guards to keep the person under guard and to prevent them from leaving, and that the prison guard also had complete knowledge of the circumstances, that the guard would also be personally liable. And we submit that the issue here is not whether the prison staff in Celebici had a duty to inquire into the circumstances of the detainees, whether they ought to have known; our submission is that they had actual knowledge. And certainly in the case of Mr. Delic, it's the Prosecution [sic] that he did have actual knowledge. If it could be shown that he didn't have any knowledge, then some issue of whether he ought to have known might arise, but that's simply not the circumstance here and that's not the Prosecution's submission. Mr. Moran also talked about the legitimate security forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina having the right to take people into custody in the middle of a long war pending a determination of their status, and my reply to Mr. Ackerman applies equally to that submission. Unless the Chamber has any further questions, I'd then move to my response to Mr. Kuzmanovic's submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. May I just have a moment to correct what I think is a misstatement by Mr. Staker and remind him that I agree the burden is on the appellant with respect to count 48. He is the appellant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, I thank my friend. In response to Mr. Kuzmanovic's submissions, if I understand correctly, there's no dispute between Mr. Kuzmanovic and the Prosecution on the standard of review on appeal where an error of fact is alleged. The standard is that of unreasonableness, and submissions have been made on this. On this particular issue, the burden is on Mr. Mucic to establish that on the evidence before it, no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion that the Trial Chamber did. Secondly, if I understand Mr. Kuzmanovic correctly, he doesn't take issue with the Trial Chamber's legal finding that a person can be found liable under Article 7(3) on the basis of de facto authority. Thirdly, I do not understand Mr. Kuzmanovic to be denying that there may have been sufficient evidence from which it could reasonably have been concluded that Mr. Mucic was the commander of the camp for some of the periods material to the indictment. At least for the sake of argument, he appeared willing to accept that there was reasonable and credible evidence that Mr. Mucic's command began in late July or early August 1992. He didn't specify precisely what this evidence might have been. We note that in paragraph 737 of the Trial Chamber's judgement, the Trial Chamber said that in his interview with the Prosecution, Mr. Mucic admitted that he had authority over the camp, at least from the 27th of July, 1992, and on the basis of that, presumably it's not disputed that, on behalf of Mr. Mucic, that the Trial Chamber might have reasonably concluded that he was the commander of the prison from that date. What is complained of by Mr. Delic is the so-called backdating of his de facto authority to May 1992. Now, there's no real dispute that it was open to the Trial Chamber to conclude that he was the commander from the 27th of July, 1992. It would follow that even if he was successful in relation to this ground of appeal, his liability would be unaffected in relation to all relevant crimes committed after that date. This would include liability for inhumane conditions under counts 46 and 47, and unlawful confinement of civilians under count 48, in respect of the period that he was the commander. Furthermore, even if successful in relation to this ground of appeal in respect of the period prior to the 27th of July, 1992, his liability would not necessarily be excluded in relation to crimes committed before that date. Our submission is that the responsibility of a commander is not just to punish [sic] crimes before they're committed, but to -- it's not just to prevent crimes before they're committed, but to punish them after they're committed. And it's true that a commander cannot prevent crimes that were committed before he or she became the commander, but a commander can punish crimes that were committed before he or she became the commander. And we submit that if the doctrine of superior responsibility did not take account of this, liability for superior responsibility in cases where the commander had no prior knowledge, and therefore no means of preventing, could be avoided simply by changing commanders after a serious crime is committed. One could imagine the case, for instance, of a very large-scale massacre. If commanders could be immediately switched after it occurred, the old commander could plead that he or she never had sufficient time to take steps to punish before he or she was removed, and the new commander could say that "The crimes were committed before I was made the commander." In our submission, if the commander knows that crimes were committed by subordinates prior to the time that he or she took up command and knows they've not been punished, he or she still has a responsibility as the commander to take the necessary measures, although we would concede that it may be relevant to sentencing that the crimes were not committed during the commander's command. The issue here is then if it's possible for any trier of fact to have concluded on the evidence that Mr. Mucic was the de facto command of the camp prior to late July 1992. The first witness whose testimony Mr. Kuzmanovic referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You'll be a little while, will you? I'm just looking at the time, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, a little longer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I have a clarification? Perhaps I heard you wrongly. You said the responsibility of a commander is not to prevent crimes before they are committed but to punish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I meant to say was there is a duty to prevent crimes before they're committed and punish them after they are. And it's conceded that a commander cannot prevent a crime that was committed before the commander became the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Okay. That's what you meant. Before he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But if he was a commander, his responsibility extends.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Can still exist to punish the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But to prevent before it's committed. I quoted you here. You said, "The responsibility of a commander is not to prevent crimes before they are committed but to punish them."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Sorry. If there was a slip of the tongue, I would like to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's not what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That's not what I meant, Your Honour. There is an obligation to prevent before the crime is committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: There is. And an obligation to punish afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes it's very clear in Article 7, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes. The point I was trying to make is that if the crime was committed before the commander became the commander, there's nothing the commander could have done to prevent the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Only in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes. In that case the commander couldn't have prevented the crime because it was committed before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You review your previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before resuming my submissions, I'd just like to clarify one point. Earlier, when replying to the submissions by Mr. Ackerman, I was referring to the burden that was on Mr. Delalic in establishing errors of fact, and my learned friend was good enough to remind me that we're the appellant in relation to that ground of appeal. I want to the clarify that of course the Prosecution accepts as the appellant in relation to that ground of appeal we bear all relevant burdens of an appellant, and to the extent that we allege errors of fact by a Trial Chamber, the burden is on us to establish unreasonableness. But conversely, it's also our submission that we are entitled to rely on facts that have been found by the Trial Chamber in its judgement, and that if in response to a ground of appeal Mr. Delalic wants to advance an argument which involves a contention that a finding of fact by the Trial Chamber was incorrect, then even as respondent the burden is on him to establish unreasonableness. I think it's clear that if he had been convicted and were now cross-appealing in this matter and part of the cross-appeal was an allegation of the error of fact, the relevant burden in that respect wouldn't be subject to any ambiguity at all. To the extent that he was alleging errors of fact, the burden would be on him. Indeed, originally in these proceedings he filed a notice of cross-appeal. It's since been clarified. Technically that wasn't a cross-appeal, they're really grounds of contention rather than grounds of appeal, but we submit that the principle is the same, that both parties are entitled to rely on and are subject to, in their submissions, the facts as found by the Trial Chamber and that either party, whether appellant or respondent, to the extent that they seek to advance arguments that rely on errors of fact in the Trial Chamber's judgement, the party advancing that argument bears of burden of establishing unreasonableness. I'll then resume my response to Mr. Kuzmanovic's submissions. The first witness whose testimony Mr. Kuzmanovic referred to is that of Witness P. In paragraph 746 of the Trial Chamber's judgement, the Trial Chamber says: "Evidence of the actual exercise of authority over the Celebici prison-camp by Zdravko Mucic was given in the testimony of Witness P, who stated that he was transferred early in June 1992 to the prison camp from the 3rd of March school by Mr. Mucic." And there's a reference in the judgement to transcript page 4518. Mr. Kuzmanovic states that when one looks at that transcript reference, the transcript never reveals that Witness P was transferred from Celebici in June 1992. The Prosecution submits that this is not what the Trial Chamber says. On that page of the transcript, Witness P describes how Mr. Mucic arrived at the 3rd of March school and told him, Witness P, that for security reasons Witness P and others had to be moved. The testimony was that Mr. Mucic read out the names of some people who were to be taken to the Musala sports hall and the name of Witness P and others who were taken to Celebici. In answer to questions in the following three pages of the transcript, the witness explains that on about the 10th of June, a few days before this transfer, Mr. Mucic had met him at the 3rd of March school and told him that he, Mr. Mucic, would soon being taking over the command of the Celebici camp. The inference which the Trial Chamber appears to have drawn from this is that by the time Mr. Mucic returned a few days later to collect Witness P and the others, he had by then become the de facto commander of Celebici. And it's submitted that the -- this reading of the Trial Chamber's judgement is confirmed by the fact that the Trial Chamber refers also to the testimony of Mirko Dordic, at transcript page 4795, as evidence of Mr. Mucic's status, and this witness there also saw Mr. Mucic arranging for the transfer of prisoners from the 3rd of March school and also testified that he first saw Mr. Mucic in June. Then there is a further reference to witness Dr. Grubac, who at transcript pages 5965 to 5968, similarly reported that Mr. Mucic transferred him from the school to the Celebici camp in early June. At paragraph 748 of its judgement, the Trial Chamber then refers to the testimony of Witness D, whom the Trial Chamber said testified that Mr. Mucic was the commander and that he had an office in the prison camp. What is most significant in relation to this witness is that the Trial Chamber said, at paragraph 762 of the judgement, by that paragraph it made express findings that the evidence of this witness was reliable and credible and that this witness was in a position to know the exact status of Mr. Mucic. This witness, Witness D, was a member of the Military Investigative Commission and testified that Mr. Mucic was the camp commander, that he had an office at the camp, and that when the commission met in early June to discuss how they would go about their work, Mr. Mucic was present. And I'd refer to transcript pages 5174, in particular to line 19; to page 5175, lines 18 to 21. Witness D further testified that when he began working with the commission in June, Mr. Mucic supplied the commission with the initial lists of the prisoners. That is transcript page 5183. And he also testified that the written documentation from the field which the commission required in order to go about its work was also kept by Mr. Mucic. That's transcript page 5188 to 5189. In addition to the evidence specifically referred to in its judgement, there was also other evidence before the Trial Chamber, not all of which were cited in detail, in relation to the finding of superior responsibility. Now, we submit that while the Trial Chamber is required to give a reasoned judgement, it's not necessarily required to refer to every item of evidence in support of a particular conclusion, and that in determining whether a reasonable Trial Chamber could reach a particular conclusion on the evidence, it's permissible to look at the evidence before it as a whole and not just the specific parts of the evidence referred to in the judgement in relation to that specific issue. There was evidence in the testimony of Witness T, who said that he was first assigned to Celebici immediately after the capture of Donje Selo. That's transcript page 6671, lines 19 to 12. And by that time frame was meant May 1992, which is clear from transcript page 6814. And he testified that a very short time after that, he was assigned duties as a driver. Again, transcript page 6657, line 25, to 6858. When he was asked who was the commander of the camp during the period he worked as a driver, he answer that Zdravko Mucic was. Transcript page 6673. Mr. Mucic's co-accused Mr. Landzo also testified that when he and a number of other soldiers were assigned to Celebici, which was in mid-June - on that I refer to transcript page 15027, lines 14 to 15 - they were met by Mr. Mucic, who then selected certain persons to become guards and explained their duties and obligations, transcript pages 15029 to 15030. And then the witness Gordana Grubac testified about a week or ten days before Dr. Grubac was released on the 22nd of July, 1992, she visited the camp, transcript page 5996. She testified that on arrival, she met a guard called Hondo, and that the guard told her that the commander Pavo was calling her and that then Pavo sent the guard to get her husband. Mr. Kuzmanovic referred to some of the witness testimony referred to in the Trial Chamber's judgement and sought to show that reliance on it was unreasonable. He argues that the testimony of particular witnesses did not prove that Mr. Mucic exercised effective control over the camp, in particular because the relevant witness concerned either placed Mr. Mucic in the camp at the relevant time but didn't identify him as the commander, or identified him as the commander but without being specific as to the relevant time. Now, our submission is that it must be evident that witness testimony of this kind can be weighed in determining the issue even if in itself it doesn't give details of every element that has to be proved. Witness testimony can be cumulative, and there was testimony of many witnesses that was relevant to this particular issue. Various witnesses, without being specific as to time, testified that Mr. Mucic was the commander of the prison. There wasn't a suggestion in this witness testimony that there was a particular time that he wasn't the commander or a particular time when he arrived and took up duties as commander. The general testimony was just that he was the commander. This general testimony, taken together with the testimony of other witnesses that place him in the camp at various times prior to the 27th of July, 1992, taken together with the other evidence I've referred to earlier, that he was the commander at an earlier period, on the basis of all this evidence, the Prosecution submits that it was open to a reasonable Trial Chamber to conclude from all of the evidence as a whole that he was the commander of the prison throughout the period. Mr. Kuzmanovic said yesterday that the Trial Chamber boasted that there was a plethora of evidence on this issue. In fact, as I read the judgement, the word "plethora" was used in paragraph 769 of the judgement in relation to the evidence of the knowledge of Mr. Mucic that guards in the camp were committing crimes against the detainees. Whether or not one describes the evidence of his de facto status as a superior earlier than July 1992 as a plethora, the Prosecution does submit that the evidence taken as a whole is sufficient, that it was possible for a reasonable Trial Chamber to have reached the conclusion on this issue that it did. The Prosecution therefore submits that this ground of appeal should be rejected, and unless the Chamber has any questions, that is the Prosecution response to their ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Staker. Does that conclude the Prosecution's reply and response?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I believe those are the Prosecution's submissions in relation to group 1 of the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Kuzmanovic, do you wish to reply to the response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, Your Honour. Mr. Morrison and I will split some very short argument on the response. And since Mr. Morrison is next to the mike, I'll let him go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my learned friend for taking me completely by surprise. My response is short and simple. It's the quality of evidence that matters, not the number of people who say it. And my learned friend, Mr. Kuzmanovic, referred to the inconsistencies yesterday. Those determine the quality of evidence. And you can have as many witnesses as you like coming along and giving partial evidence, and all that partiality does not up to quality. And it's a matter for determination by this learned Appeal Chamber as to whether or not looking at that testimony in the round, it is evidence which on the face of it is quality evidence, and our submission is that it is not. And if one looks in particular at the evidence that we hope -- I jump a large gun -- if one looks at the evidence which we hope, or the information which we hope that will be before the Appellate Chamber in due course as to the de jure date of appointment, that will cast even greater doubt upon the veracity and quality of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My colleague, Mr. Staker, framed the issue that whether it's possible for any trier of fact to have concluded on the evidence that Mr. Mucic was de facto commander prior to the date of July 1992. It's my submission that possibility does not rise to the standard of beyond a reasonable doubt. It's not sufficient to rise to that standard. Anything is possible, as you all well know, but the standard is beyond a reasonable doubt. The other issue is the reasonableness, as I discussed yesterday, and as Mr. Staker and I have debated what that reasonableness or unreasonableness is. When there are competing inferences to be made from testimony, we submit that it is unreasonable, and may, in fact, be a miscarriage of justice, to make every single one of those inferences against the accused. And that's what it seems the judgement does in those sections relating to Mr. Mucic on the issue of command responsibility, specifically backdating, as Mr. Staker framed it and as I think is an accurate statement, the backdating of de facto command back to May of 1992. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Well, that disposes of the first group of grounds of appeal somewhat later than we expected, and we now turn to group 2. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's obvious, Your Honours, that we are running significantly behind the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's not an invitation for you to speak any more quickly, though, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. However, I intend to do my part to assist us in getting caught up by being quite brief on this issue, and at the same time encouraging all my colleagues to join me in an effort to try and get us caught up. We haven't even finished the first day yet, according to the schedule. The point that's raised with regard to Common Article 3 is very extensively set out in the brief that we have filed with the Chamber. This is only relevant as regards Mr. Delalic if this Chamber decides that there should be a retrial or some other disposition that would implicate his criminal liability under Article 3 of the Statute. Co-defendants Delic and Mucic, however, have adopted that portion of Mr. Delalic's brief, and as a result it is important to them whether or not there is a retrial. What you're clearly being asked to do, Your Honours, is revisit the decision of a prior Appeals Chamber, that being the decision arrived at in the Tadic jurisdictional decision. Recently in the Aleksovski appeals judgement, the Appeals Chamber discussed at some length this issue of when, if ever, it might be appropriate to depart from its own precedent. As it was made clear in that decision, departure from precedent should only occur in the interests of justice. I submit that it's clearly without question an injustice when individuals are convicted for violating a law which does not exist in international criminal jurisprudence, and I suggest to you that that's the case with Common Article 3. In my brief -- and I rely on my brief for the argument regarding the statutory interpretation that somehow allowed Common Article 3 to find its way into Article 3 of the Statute. As you all know, it is not specifically mentioned in Article 3; it's not even alluded to in any way in Article 3. It seems to me that it's virtually conclusive that it was not intended by the Security Council to be within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, in Article 3 or anywhere else, when one looks at the statement of the Secretary-General of the United Nations upon the adoption of the Rwanda Statute, where he said that Common Article 3 was being criminalised for the very first time. He wouldn't have said that had he believed that it was part of this Tribunal's Statute. So the question becomes: Was the Tadic Appeals Chamber wrong? Was that wrongly decided by the Tadic Appeals Chamber? And I suggest to you that the answer is clearly yes. It was a decision that I suggest to you was given in per curiam. You do not see in that decision anything like the rigorous analysis required for establishing that a principle has entered into customary international law, nor do you see that kind of a rigorous analysis in the dicta that appears in the Nicaragua decision that was relied upon to some extent in the Tadic jurisdictional decision. Very simplified, but I think to the point, customary international law is that which the nations of the world at any given moment believe to be the law and consider themselves to be bound by. The difficulty is deriving what that sense of the International Community is, or was, with regard to Common Article 3 in 1992. This Chamber, or any Chamber, must not guess at that, but may only conclude that a principle is customary international law if they find that to be so beyond doubt. The very last time that the International Community prior to 1992 had an opportunity to express their position with regard to Common Article 3 was upon its adoption in 1949, and it's very clear that in 1949, when the nations of the world had that opportunity to express their view about it, that that view was that it was not a matter of international criminal law. The grave breaches scheme was adopted as a matter of international criminal law, and individual criminal responsibility was provided for that. But because there was a large concern regarding sovereignty, none of those nations were willing to have that same grave breaches scheme applied to themselves in internal armed conflicts, and therefore there was no grave breaches scheme adopted with regard to internal armed conflicts. There was simply a statement of principle, and that statement of principle is what became Common Article 3. The Tadic interlocutory appeal decision came about very early on in the life of this Tribunal. There is no indication that that issue was properly and fully briefed for that court, or properly and fully presented to that Tribunal. It was really only decided in an interlocutory fashion to guide the Trial Chamber in Tadic through the Tadic trial. There is no indication that the Chamber was even made aware of the many matters contained in our brief, including the statement of the Secretary-General upon the adoption of the Rwanda Statute. We recognise that departing from that decision by the Tadic interlocutory appeal Chamber is a very difficult step to take, since so much of what has gone before in this Tribunal has relied upon that decision. It is tempting, I know, to consider the result of a decision you might make, the impact that that might have, but a result-oriented Tribunal is destined to make bad law. The post World War II tribunals were justifiably criticised for fashioning the law to fit the facts. All we can ask with regard to this issue is that you give it very careful consideration and ignore, as Judges must ignore, the impact that decision may have, but make the decision based upon whether your analysis, your own analysis of this matter, will justify in your own minds that Common Article 3 really is part of customary international law. I think our brief shows that it is not. That concludes my remarks on that section, Your Honour, and let me suggest to you that as we move to the next group, where I am scheduled to talk about the protected persons issue, I will not, in the interests of time and for other reasons. I have spoken very briefly about it in my remarks regarding count 48, and I believe that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Actually, we're moving on to group 4 after this, but we'll bear in mind you don't want to say anything in support, anything orally, in support of the protected persons point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope that I can be even briefer and refer principally simply to our written submissions. Our position is that we rely on the principles of precedent as have now been set out in the Aleksovski appeal judgement. Our response brief also contains a section dealing with principles of precedent in this Tribunal. It would be our submission that the findings made in the Aleksovski appeal judgement are basically in accord with the submissions we make, and that remains our position. Our submission would be that the Tadic jurisdiction appeal was not a decision that was given in per incuriam, as I understand that expression. The Appeals Chamber did focus specifically on this issue. The arguments were extensive and many authorities were referred to. Mr. Ackerman argues that the reasoning in that decision was not sufficiently rigorous and invites the Appeals Chamber to decide if in its own analysis Common Article 3 is really customary international law, and in our submission, that's precisely what the Aleksovski appeal judgement says that an Appeals Chamber should not do in relation to precedent. It may be that in the case of decisions of many supreme courts in jurisdictions there may be commentators who take the view that the reasoning of the Court may not have been as rigorous as it might have been, but that's not a reason for that same appellate jurisdiction to depart from its own previous decision in subsequent cases. We submit that something more compelling than that is needed. As Mr. Ackerman pointed out, the Tadic jurisdiction decision was given early on the Tribunal's history, which means it's relatively long standing as a precedent in the history of this Tribunal, and that there have been numerous subsequent cases that have relied on it, not only final judgements but also interlocutory decisions relating to defects in the form of the indictment, and trials do proceed on the basis that the Tadic jurisdiction appeal is correct. It's also our submission that the more long standing a precedent is, the more reliance that has been placed on it, the more reluctant the Appeals Chamber should be to depart from what has now become the settled law of this Tribunal. Those are my submissions, if the Chamber pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Could we have a translation of this by somebody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I will try to ask my question again. I'll try again to -- I see that we have a translation, so I'll ask my question. I have two questions. One question I want to ask to the Prosecution and the other one to the Defence counsel. It's about Article 3. First my question to the Prosecutor, since he's standing. I would like to know, you are relying on the Tadic decision in the interlocutory appeal. I would like to know how you justify that Article 3, Common Article 3 to the Geneva Conventions. How do you justify that this Article can be the basis for individual criminal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer may not sound intellectually satisfying, but it's genuinely put that the Appeals Chamber, in its earlier decision, so found and that is now the settled law of the Tribunal. To give a substantive answer to the question, in my submission, would amount to a reopening of that decision and an examining of the merits, and that is precisely what, in our submission, the Appeals Chamber should not be willing to do in the absence of more compelling reason. We would simply, as we said in our brief, adopt the reasoning that was put forward by the Appeals Chamber in that case and rely on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but still you can answer my question without hiding behind the Tadic case. My question is: What are the arguments that push you to -- that lead you to base individual criminal responsibility on Common Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: If I could take a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as it has been our submission that we do rely on precedent, if Your Honour would want an answer on the substance of this question, we'd request leave to perhaps address this after the next break briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, you can, if you like, answer later on. I'd like to make my question very specific. It's about a case when you have an armed conflict that is an international armed conflict, when it is characterised as an international armed conflict, because when you have internal conflicts, the situation is slightly simpler, because in that case, we can rely on the Statute of the Rwanda Tribunal. Now I'm going to turn to Defence counsels. I believe it's Mr. Ackerman I should ask this question to. Okay. First question about stare decisis. You said that an Appeals Chamber can modify its decision in the interests of justice in quoting Aleksovski. Well, in Aleksovski it is said, but you went a bit fast. You said that the interests of justice in Aleksovski is seen as the end result. You said it can change its decision -- since we don't have the translation in English, I'm going to quote: [In English] Cogent reasons in the interests of justice. [Interpretation] So what's important, it's not the interests of justice but cogent reasons. And the objective, of course, is the interests of justice, according to you. And that's my first question. According to you, what are the cogent reasons, these imperative reasons that should lead us to change our opinion about the Tadic case as an Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're correct that that's exactly what the Aleksovski case provides. And when you begin to look at what is in the interest of justice, what is a cogent reason in the interest of justice, what you look for is whether the Tadic decision is creating a manifest injustice, and I suggest to you that it is a manifest injustice if persons are being convicted of serious crimes and sentenced to serve serious time in gaol pursuant to an analysis that is flawed and which gives this Tribunal apparent jurisdiction under Common Article 3. If this Tribunal does not have that jurisdiction, and I think it's fairly clear in the brief that I've filed and in any kind of a rigorous analysis that one makes under the principles that one normally uses to arrive at what is customary international law, I think it's clear that Common Article 3 does not meet that test. There simply is no -- there is no opinio juris. There is nothing out there. The best the Tadic Trial Chamber could do was come up with a couple of newspaper reports of a couple of cases in Nigeria where some people had been prosecuted for murder, but even then it wasn't clear that Common Article 3 had nothing to do with those prosecutions. The only other thing they came up with was there were a couple of military manuals which indicated that Common Article 3 could play a role in court martials, but that's a long way from the community of nations considering themselves to be bound by the provisions of Common Article 3 in the sense that individual criminal responsibility could result from violation of them. And that's where it all really breaks down, is where you start looking at the issue of individual criminal responsibility. It seems to me that it is a cogent reason, in the interest of justice, to re-examine that when people are being convicted and sentenced to prison under a theory that doesn't hold any water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. My second question is the following: You're telling us that Common Article 3 is not part of customary international law and about customary law as such. We have a great deal of case law, international case law about that that we can rely on, and you're perfectly familiar with that. So that's my question. What about this international case law that considers that Common Article 3 is part of the basis of that? You have a number of case law to rely on about that. Now, about Geneva Conventions and the incrimination under the Geneva Conventions. You tell us it's only valid for grave breaches that are a matter of customary international law. As you know, grave violations in the Geneva Convention, that's a notion that is normally to be used in international conflicts in order to grant a universal judicial jurisdiction to all Tribunals on any person who has committed such violations, but it does not mean that beyond that universal jurisdiction, based on grave breaches, grave violation, it does not mean that the states have not set up other things. And this has been recognised in the case law of the Tribunal for violations of the laws and customs of war, and it's Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal. So my question is: What do you make then of Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying is Article 3, about breaches of the laws or customs of war, and you are perfectly aware of that Article. You have Article 2 with grave breaches, but Article 3 of the Statute. I'm not talking about Common Article 3, I'm talking about Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal. So what do you make of Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if one looks at the report of the secretary general upon the establishment of this Tribunal, the Secretary-General first points out that this Tribunal should only deal with matters that are, without question, parts of customary international law or treaty law, and in that context, the Secretary-General mentions, I believe, three or four things. One of those is the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and its grave breaches scheme; one of those is the Hague law; one of those is the charter of the Nuremberg Tribunal, suggesting that each of those has arrived at the status of customary international law. So if you look at the Articles that resulted from that analysis, you find, in Article 2, the law of Geneva, and you find in Article 3 the law of The Hague. And if you look at what is specifically set out in Article 3 as what are violations of that Article, those things all derive from the 1907 Hague Convention. To suggest, Your Honour, it seems to me that somehow it was the intention of the Security Council and the Secretary-General that that Article also pick up a number of other matters that this Tribunal might decide is within its jurisdiction is improper I think all it meant in the residual clause in Article 3 was other provisions of the 1907 Hague Convention that weren't specifically stated there. It is, in my mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you. So you mean that Article 3 has nothing to do with the competence, the jurisdiction of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Article 3 limits that jurisdiction, I think, Your Honour, to Hague law, what's generally referred to as Hague law. It is -- let me take just a moment on the issue of statutory construction, where you have a criminal Statute which says: "It shall be unlawful to do the following", among other things, "do the following." That leads one to conclude that maybe there are some other things that could be criminalised by that, but that is not a way a criminal statute should be drafted for it to be valid.
