A criminal statute which says, "You shall not do a following thing and a few others that we haven't thought about yet" is not a statute that should survive, and especially when, if you look at a statute like Article 3, which has some very specific things in it, there is nothing in there, in the specific part of that Statute that even approaches the seriousness of the offence of murder, and it seems bizarre to me that the Security Council would write you a statute that basically contains a listing of certain things that should not be done in a conflict and would leave out something as serious as murder. So I just don't know how you take a statute with that kind of limited coverage and limited nature of the offences covered in there and put an even more severe -- and then graft an even more severe offence on top of it like murder and not violate the principle of nullem crimen sine lege, if nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, my recollection of the charter annexed to the London agreement included imposing personal responsibility upon those who acted in breach of a treaty. You don't think that that might be some sort of a clue as to how we could interpret Article 3, which, after all, does say such violations shall include but not be limited to The Hague matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The way I read that is, "Such violations may include but not be limited to The Hague matters that we have set out in this Article."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see, the Geneva Conventions, I suppose, can be regarded as a treaty, can't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, they can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And if back in 1945 it was thought to be part of the customary law that you could have personal responsibility imposed for a breach of a treaty, why can't there be a breach of Common Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For breach of the grave breaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. No, of Common Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this Tribunal, like anyone else, must analyse its jurisdiction in terms of what is customary international law, and there is a rigorous procedure that must go through to get to that point. What I'm suggesting is Common Article 3 is not customary international law and never has been. I do understand your point, that it was part of the Nuremberg thing, but that's not where this Tribunal has said it is; it's said it's in Article 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're asking us, however, to revisit it, and I just put that up for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you to revisit it, and I've answered you as best I can at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you showed some surprise as to the -- let us say the non-serious crimes which Article 3 refers to, and where it says "but not be limited to," and you are astonished that it did not mention war crimes, like murder or that sort. Did I understand you rightly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you think if the word "but not be limited to," don't you think that could extend to the more serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's my contention, Your Honour, that when you put a catch-all phrase like that in, it certainly can't be intended that it reach out and catch more serious crimes than those already set out in the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would rather conclude that it should not be extended to catch lighter crimes. But serious crimes, you know, they say in French, "qui peut le plus peur le moins." So if I really can punish light crimes, my hand can't reach more serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think, unless you run afoul of the principle of nullem crimen sine lege, and that's what I think this tends to run afoul of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The principle of nullem crimen sine lege would not apply here, because if wounding a person is a crime, killing him is definitely a crime, even without having to -- you can't oppose the principle of nullem crimen for a more serious crime. You can oppose it to a lighter crime, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, we get into what is a really kind of sticky wicket, and that is: Clearly, killing someone is a crime in every national jurisdiction. There's no question about that. Murder is a malum in se offence. So it's not a question of whether murder is an offence; the question is whether that murder, committed in that international conflict, is subject to Prosecution in this Tribunal as an offence against international criminal law or only subject to Prosecution by the authorities in the country in which that murder was committed. I would never suggest to you that a murderer go free; only that the jurisdiction of this Tribunal is limited, and it's limited to the extent that it is not international law to prosecute someone for what is a murder committed in an international armed conflict aside from the grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Just a small question following on what has been said up to now on this matter. What will be your position as to considering that Article 3, Common Article 3, would be applicable to international conflicts in substance, in light of Article 75 of the Additional Protocol 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That more or less is based on the same provision that Common Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Geneva Conventions very clearly set up a scheme for prosecuting murder and similar offences in international armed conflicts, so that Common Article 3, it's not necessary to even consider whether it might apply to an international armed conflict or not, because that already exists within the grave breaches provisions of the Geneva Convention to cover international armed conflicts. It's only in the internal armed conflict that there is that issue, it seems to me. Have I answered your question or did I misinterpret it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: My question was that later on, after the Geneva Conventions, when the Additional Protocol was adopted, Article 75 of that protocol is based exactly on Common Article 3 and it applies to international armed conflicts. The wording itself is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I find myself in Mr. Staker's position. I'll have to do a little bit of looking before I can legitimately answer that question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. We'll look forward to hearing from you about that one later. Mr. Moran, you've got issue 3 to deal with, which is an associated ground here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Your Honour. This issue is basically whether or not the four Geneva Conventions applied into Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to 31 December 1992, when the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina became parties to these treaties. I think we can all agree in this room that a government, any government, has the right to join a treaty, join an international convention, or not join an international convention. We can also all in this room agree that the government, when it joins an international convention or a bilateral treaty, can make it binding upon itself retroactively for state responsibility. The question is: Can that government, or can anyone, make an act criminal under an international convention prior to the time that international convention became effective? My position would be that would be a violation of nullem crimen and what we in the United States would call ex post facto laws. An ex post facto law is any kind of law that makes an action done before the passage of the law, and which was innocent before it was done, criminal and punishes it, or every law that aggravates a crime or makes it greater than it was when the act was committed, every law that increases the punishment, and every law that changes the legal rules of evidence and receives less or different testimony than the law required at the time of the commission in order to convict. Your Honour, I propose that those principles are common throughout the world. In our brief we cited, courtesy of Professor Bassiouni, dozens and dozens of legal systems and constitutions. Applying it to this case, every act alleged in the indictment occurred prior to 31 December 1992, at the time that Bosnia-Herzegovina became parties to the Conventions. The Prosecutor alleges in his brief, asserts, that the four Geneva Conventions are customary international law. My response to that is: Prove it. The International Court of Justice in the North Sea Continental Shelf cases, and others which I've cited in my brief, say that a party asserting that something is customary international law has the obligation to show that it is. They haven't. Also, if it's customary international law, even if they have proven it, this Tribunal would have jurisdiction under Article 3, not Article 2, to punish and hear violations of customary international law. I think we've all agreed to that. And there's one other factor that I think is very important related to the date that Bosnia-Herzegovina became a party to the Conventions, and that is -- Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm going to stop you to make something clear. It's a very straightforward point. You said on the 31st of December, 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina became party to the Geneva Conventions. Do you know how Bosnia-Herzegovina became party to the Geneva Conventions on the 31st of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I understand it, they filed with the -- I believe it's with the Swiss government, articles that they were to become a party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, there are many ways of becoming party to conventions. You can ratify a convention after signing it, you can become -- adhere to a convention if you have not signed it before. But there's another way to be party of a convention. It's using the principle of succession. I suppose you're aware of that, of that way of becoming party to a convention. You succeed to another state, a state you were a part of, Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I've asked for the text, the document related to that in the report of the Red Cross -- or sorry, the Swiss Federal Council, rather. Bosnia-Herzegovina became party to the Conventions on the 31st of December based on the principle of succession. Does it not mean something when you become part of a convention as part of a succession principle? You simply declare that you secede the state of Yugoslavia when it comes to the duties and obligations, legal duties and obligations enshrined in the Geneva Conventions. Don't you think that this fact is important and to be taken into account?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's an important fact as to the state responsibilities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not just Bosnia-Herzegovina, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we are not going to dwell on that much further. I'm not doing an exam here about that. But I think it has a consequence in terms of international law. The seceding country is considered as having become part of the Convention from the time it has become a state, so there is no break in the membership, in the fact of being part to this Convention. There is no break in the duties you have under the Conventions. That's what it means when you secede another state. It's a sort of inheritance. You inherit what comes to you from the previous state. There used to be a state before. In that particular case, there has been a number of states that have been created, that have become independent and separated themselves from one state, but there is no break in terms of the duties you have under the Convention. There is a continuity. And as a consequence, Bosnia, at the time of the facts we are interested in, was binded by the Conventions. So that alters slightly your argumentation, because this argument as such is not very important because it's part of the customary law. But if you look at the conventional argument, since we are talking about the notion of succession here, I don't think it has any weight here. But I'm finished with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just, I think, answer that a little bit. First, there is some confusion -- or not confusion so much as disagreement as to state succession involving the Former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. For instance, the nations, the seceding states, the successor states, the parts of the SFRY that broke off, either have been admitted to the United Nations General Assembly as new states or they have not been admitted at all. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that's Serbian Montenegro, takes the position that they are the successor state to the SFRY, and the Security Council has consistently rejected that. Setting that aside, this question still remains: Can the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by taking a position on December 31st, 1992 with the Swiss Federal Council that we are the successor to the SFRY and we are becoming parties to the Conventions, as successor to the SFRY, create criminal liability on individual persons in international law for grave breaches of the Conventions for the period between the time that Bosnia became an independent state and it became party to the conventions. There is that period of time where Bosnia-Herzegovina was silent as to its status under the conventions, and that's the period of time we're focussing on in this trial. Your Honour, there is one other issue that this immediately brings to mind of whether or not Bosnia was a party, and that is this: Article 4 of the Geneva Convention relative to civilians, among its other definitions and exclusions, specifically says that nationals of a state which are not parties to this convention are not protected by it. If there is no criminal liability imposed during this period between April and December 1992, when Bosnia-Herzegovina had not become a party to the Conventions, at least during that period, the nationals of Bosnia were not nationals of a state which was a party to the Convention, can you retroactively make them protected persons? And my suggestion to you is: Again you run into a nullem crimen problem. You're making an act illegal that occurred prior to the time of the Statute, and I don't think you can do that. Your Honour, unless there is further questions from the bench, I'm going to give some time back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll take the lunch break now and resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the delay. One of our members is also the duty Judge. Mr. Farrell, your turn?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: You'll be happy to know it is, I'm sure, but in the meantime, I understand that Mr. Staker would like to attempt to address Judge Bennouna's question if he may at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: On the previous appeal point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber, prior to the last break, Judge Bennouna asked me a question raising a matter of substantive law in relation to Common Article 3. Our original intention had been to rely on the doctrine of precedent. As we said, this avoids reopening issues that have already been decided and going into matters of substance, but having asked the question, we do wish to assist the bench to the best of our ability. Like any issue of substantive law though, questions such as these are no doubt capable of a short answer or a long answer, and not knowing quite how long an answer might be required, I thought that Chamber might best be assisted if I called on my colleague, Ms. Sonja Boelaert-Suominen, to answer this question, who would then be in a position to answer any follow-up questions that might arise. So with the leave of the Chamber, I would call on my colleague to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the first time for me to appear before the Appeals Chamber. I'd like to say it's an honour. If I may address your question, Judge Bennouna. The question you asked this morning, if I understand it correctly, is the following: Why is it that the Prosecution believes that the Tadic jurisdiction decision regarding the scope of Article 3 of the Statute and its inclusion of Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions should be followed? Now, as my colleague Christopher Staker told, it is not an answer that can be given in a few minutes, so I will quickly run down through the points which were discussed by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic jurisdiction decision, and if there's any point in time a reason for you to ask a question, you can interrupt me and I will try to answer the question. Now, when you look at the Tadic jurisdiction decision, the Appeals Chamber examined various questions. There's a question of substance; namely, is there conduct, for instance, an act or omission, which is prohibited under international law? Secondly, there is the question of criminality. If a certain conduct is prohibited, does that lead to individual criminal responsibility? Thirdly, there is a question of jurisdiction. Is there any court, for instance, this court, which has jurisdiction over that offence? Now, as we all know, the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic jurisdiction decision examined at length the scope of the various Articles of the Statute, but the Articles which we are concerned with today are Articles 2 and 3 the Statute. If you look at the Statute, Article 3, on the face of it, only deals with grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions. Sorry, Article 2. Article 3, on the face of it, only deals with the violations of laws or customs of war. Now, to most observers that would be a reference to the violations of The Hague conventions of 1907, but in the Tadic jurisdiction decision, the Appeals Chamber decided that for various reasons, Article 2 should be interpreted restrictively but Article 3 should be given a broad scope. It has decided that it should not only cover violations of the 1907 Hague Conventions but also a host of other treaties and customary rules of international law. If you allow me, I'll quickly run through the list. So the Appeals Chamber decided that Article 3 of the Statute covers not only violations of The Hague convention but also infringements of the Geneva Conventions not mentioned in Article 2, which refers to grave breaches. The Appeals Chamber also decided that Article 3 of the Statute also covers violations of Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and also violations of other agreements binding on the parties to the conflict by reasons of treaty law. Now, the Appeals Chamber decided that Article 3 should be given a broad scope for the reason that, in its opinion, Article 3 was aimed at making the provisions of the Statute watertight, so that no serious violation of international law would escape the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. So that is for the question of scope, the relationship between Article 2 and Article 3. For us, we have been using Article 3 as indicated by the Appeals Chamber as a residual provision. We can use it as indicated by the Appeals Chamber, every time we have conduct that doesn't fall under Article 2, Article 4, or Article 5 of the Statute. Now, as regards for the question which Judge Bennouna posed this morning: Why is it that the Prosecutor believes that Common Article 3 can be used in situations such as we have today in the Celebici case, where there is, in the Prosecutor's submission, an international armed conflict? Now, that is not only a question of substance but also a question of criminality. Now, in the Tadic jurisdiction decision in 1995, the Appeals Chamber stated that, as has been held before by the International Court of Justice, Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions does not only apply in internal armed conflict. It is true when the Geneva Conventions were enacted in 1949 that the drafters thought of Common Article 3 as a provision specifically enacted to deal with internal armed conflict. But in 1984, in the Nicaragua case, the International Court of Justice reasoned that if Common Article 3 applies to internal conflict and gives expression to the elementary considerations of humanity that apply in internal armed conflict, they surely should also apply in international armed conflict. It cannot be that something which is prohibited in internal armed conflict would be allowed in international armed conflict. And from then onwards it has been generally accepted that Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions gives expression to elementary considerations of humanity that apply across the board, regardless of the character of the conflict. This is why the Prosecution believes that even in a situation as in the Celebici case, where we think that the conflict is an international one, that we can rely on violations of Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. Briefly put, it is because it is now generally accepted that Common Article 3 gives expression to elementary considerations of humanity that apply regardless of the character of the conflict. Now, finally, I would briefly like to state something about the question of criminality. Before the Tadic jurisdiction decision, there had not been any decision rendered by an International Tribunal stating clearly that persons could be prosecuted for violations of Common Article 3. But that in itself does not raise any question of the principle of legality. Because as one noted commentator stated, if violations of the international laws of war have traditionally been regarded as criminal under international law, there is no reason of principle why once those laws came to be extended to the context of internal armed conflicts, their violation in that context should not have been criminal, at least in the absence of clear indications to the contrary. Finally, I would like to make a reference to the case of Regina versus R, which was decided in 1991 by the House of Lords in the case of marital rape. It is in that case which was dealt with by the European Court of Human Rights in 1995, where the principle was clearly stated that the principle of legality does not preclude development of criminal law, for instance, through jurisprudence, so long as those developments do not criminalise conduct which at the time it was committed could reasonably have been regarded as legitimate. So the reasoning which should be applied in this case is that there was no doubt that when the Appeals Chamber rendered its decision in 1995, in the Tadic jurisdiction decision, that conduct prescribed by Common Article 3 was illegitimate, regardless of the character of the conflict. The fact that the Appeals Chamber in 1995 clearly stated that persons who perpetrate violations of Common Article 3 can be prosecuted before this Tribunal does not raise the question of the principle of legality. That would be the substance of what the Prosecution would like to submit in trying to answer the question posed by Mr. Bennouna this morning. Judge Bennouna, does it answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have indeed. Thank you very much. But there is one additional piece of information that you have not mentioned. The fact that we find ourselves within the framework of an International Tribunal, and the fact that these kinds of violations are being prosecuted by an international tribunal, do these facts have any impact or any influence on individual criminal responsibility as defined by Common Article 3? Let me make this a bit clearer, if I can. The Geneva Conventions do not -- did not at the time think about the possibility of the establishment of an international tribunal. They could only foresee grave breaches of Geneva Conventions within the framework of which people belonging to a particular country could be judged in a country that they were not a citizen of, and that's the reason why the jurisdiction was very limited. Common Article 3 was meant to apply in cases of armed internal conflict but by the jurisdictions of the country that was at cause. But when we find ourselves in the context of an international tribunal such as this one, a tribunal which was created by the International Community via a decision that is binding on all states, is there a difference that then appears? Is there a change that must be then taken into account as far as individual criminal responsibility is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: In answering your question, Your Honour, I would like to point out the following: When in 1949 the Geneva Conventions were enacted, you are quite correct in stating that the States enacting the Geneva Conventions only thought that in the case of grave breaches there would be some sort of universal jurisdiction. Now, when you look at the grave breaches provision, actually they are the most, I think, concise statement of what we know as universal jurisdiction today. It obligates States, parties to the Geneva Conventions, to either prosecute the perpetrator of the grave breach violation or to extradite him to any other State that makes a prima facie case. Now, we are now in the year 2000 and public opinion and customary law have developed to such an extent that we can no longer accept that other serious violations of international humanitarian law would not be subject to the same principles, and that is the way I would put the exercise of jurisdiction which we are doing here before the Tribunal today. By enacting the Statute in 1993, the drafters of the Statute clearly intended to convey the message that the world can no longer accept these types of serious violations of international humanitarian law. And to answer your question of jurisdiction, as you know, under our Statute the Tribunal does not have exclusive jurisdiction; it has primary jurisdiction. And we are only here today because when the Security Council enacted the Statute, it thought it was necessary to send the message to the fighting parties that if they do not do their duties and do not prosecute perpetrators of serious violations of international humanitarian law, then it's the duty of the international public opinion to take up that duty. So our jurisdiction is not exclusive. So to summarise my answer, it is really true that since 1949, customary law and international humanitarian law have developed to such an extent that we can now state today that universal jurisdiction does not only exist when you are dealing with grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions but also with all kinds of other types of serious violations of international humanitarian law. And that is why the Appeals Chamber, in 1995, in the Tadic jurisdiction decision, could confidently state that actions prohibited by Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions constitute a serious violation of international humanitarian law. It leads to individual criminal responsibility and this Tribunal has jurisdiction. Not exclusive -- sorry, not primary -- it has primary jurisdiction but not exclusive. So eventually, is the States where the acts have been perpetrated do their duties and prosecute perpetrators of serious violations of International Humanitarian Law, there might be a time when this Tribunal is going to say, "We have done our task." But that is the way I would answer your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much. One last thing, since you are standing. It seems to me that a moment ago, your colleague said that the line of reasoning followed in the Tadic decision in the interlocutory appeal was not rigorous enough. Do you share that opinion that was voiced by your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SOUMINEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm bit confused. You're referring to the submission by counsel for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I am referring to something by -- that was said by a member of the Prosecution team, if I'm not mistaken, who said that the findings were quite legitimate but the reasoning behind them was not rigorous enough. I'm referring again to the Tadic appeal. Now, what is your view on the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SOUMINEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to let my colleague Chris Staker answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should perhaps simply clarify what I was intending to convey by that comment. I wasn't intending to suggest that the decision in the Tadic decision was not rigourus enough. I was simply trying to convey that under the doctrine of precedent as pronounced in the Aleksovski decision, it wouldn't be a sufficient reason to reconsider an earlier decision that some people felt perhaps, even individual Judges personally might feel, that the reasoning could have been more rigorous. We submit that under the doctrine of precedent in Aleksovski, there must be a much more compelling reason. We don't suggest that we consider the reasoning is not rigorous enough, and we're not suggesting that others don't consider it rigorous enough, although, obviously my colleagues for the Defence have made that submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a response to Judge Pocar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can we just deal with one thing at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought we were finished with this. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not sure. Let's find out. Is that the final part from the Prosecution in answer to Judge Bennouna's comments?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SOUMINEN
utterances.text: Yes. These are the final submissions of the Prosecution in response to the question posed by Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We're very grateful to you for your help.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SOUMINEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. We'll deal with you and then we'll come back to -- Mr. Farrell, was it? Yes, we'll come back to Mr. Farrell then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First of all, I want to respond just very, very briefly to what we just heard, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we can't have these submissions going on forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you want to put something to us which is brief, I suppose put so seductively, we'll listen to you, but if it isn't going to be brief, I think we're going to stop you. It was a matter raised in reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Extraordinarily brief. The Prosecutor just said that the reason for applying Common Article 3 was that it would not make sense to have something that applies in an internal conflict not also apply in an international conflict, and clearly in an international conflict, with regard to murder, you have the grave breaches, so there's not a void in an international conflict that can be filled by internal conflict law, and in this case, the Tribunal found that this was an international armed conflict, so the grave breaches should be sufficient. With regard to Judge Pocar's question. As I understand the question, it was: What was the effect, Mr. Ackerman, of Article 75 of Protocol 1? I think it is this -- I have not had a great deal of time to consider it, but I think the answer is this, Your Honour: The defendants in the Celebici case were charged under and pursuant to the language of Common Article 3. In the process of determining whether or not Common Article 3 is customary international law, one may consult a number of sources, and one of those sources that may be consulted is Article 75 of Protocol 1. That may aid someone trying to analyse whether or not it has become part of customary international law. Secondly, one must not [Realtime translation omitted the word "not"] read a provision like Article 75 out of its context. Protocol 1 is specifically directed to international armed conflicts. Protocol 2 was specifically directed to internal armed conflicts. And what is revealed when you read both of them and in their context is that between 1974 and 1977, when these Protocols were considered, it was suggested that Protocol 2 extend the reach of Common Article 3. There were 47 Articles proposed, which would have extended the reach of Common Article 3. The nations considering Protocol 2 were extraordinarily uncomfortable with that, on the same basis that they had been uncomfortable with that whole proposition back when the 1949 conventions were adopted, and that had to do with sovereignty. So only 28 of the Articles were, in fact, adopted that were proposed at that time, and in the process, the reach of Common Article 3 was made more restrictive than it had been up to that point. The Protocol 2 makes certain that removed from the coverage of Common Article 3 are situations of internal disturbances and tensions such as riots, isolated and sporadic acts of violence, and other acts of a similar nature as being not armed conflicts, which was not a limitation at the time of Common Article 3 but now is as a result of Protocol 2. In the short time that I've had to consider your question, that's the best I can do. If you would like a more extensive response and you would permit it, I would be happy to file something within a short time in writing. I would refer the Chamber to our brief in this regard. This whole issue is discussed at some length on pages 26 and 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Farrell, you are going to respond to Mr. Moran's submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ackerman. Please check the transcript there they have I think missed the word "not." You say: It should be -- it should "not" be read out of its context. It should "not" be read. They said it should be read out of its context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It should not be read out of its context. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You better check it and put in the word "not." It changes the whole sense. You should check. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we have now cleared it up with the subsequent reference that what I meant was it should not be read out of its context. Thank you, Your Honour, very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be making a few brief comments to attempt to assist the Court. In response to the Defence ground of appeal regarding Mr. Delic's issue 3 regarding the application of the Geneva Conventions. His position, as I understand it, is that the Geneva Conventions are not customary international law and, therefore, do not bind either the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina or its nationals from the time of independence until the time of the actual depositing of an instrument of secession, which was the 31st of December. It's the position of the Prosecution that Bosnia-Herzegovina was bound both by customary international law and as a result of their instrument of secession deposited on the 31st of December, 1992 with the depository state Switzerland, with the impact that the application of the Geneva Conventions took effect on the date of independence, which was March the 6th. With respect to the submission by my learned colleague that the Geneva Conventions are either not customary international law or have not been proved to be customary international law, I would simply indicate that the Prosecution relies on, first of all, the report of the Secretary-General pursuant to paragraph 2 of the Security Council Resolution 808 for the establishment of the Tribunal, which finds that there are, beyond any doubt, certain rules of International Humanitarian Law that are part of customary law. So that the problem of adherence of some but not all states to specific conventions does not arise. And one of the conventions that is referred to in the report of the Secretary-General is the Geneva Convention of August 12, 1949 and the Geneva Conventions. Secondly, support for the proposition that the Geneva Conventions are a part of customary law, which the Prosecution submits is quite evident, can also be found in the International Court of Justice's case, the nuclear weapons case, at paragraph 81, wherein the International Court of Justice indicates that there are fundamental rules that are observed by all states whether or not they have ratified the conventions that contain them because they constitute intransgressible principles of international customary law. The International Court of Justice, in fact, relies on the report of the Secretary-General, which I've just submitted to you, and concludes as well that the Geneva Conventions are part of conventional international law which have, beyond a doubt, become part of customary law. A few other references from the Tribunal itself, although they are not the Appeals Chamber in form. The Tadic decision of 7th of May, 1997, paragraph 577. In referring to the Tadic Appeals Chamber's decision, the jurisdictional decision, states: "Implicit in the Appeals Chamber decision is the conclusion that the Geneva Conventions are part of customary international law and as such their application in the present case does not violate the principle of nullem crimen sine lege." In Trial Chamber III, in the Prosecutor versus Simic et al., on a decision on a Prosecution motion dated the 27th of July, 1999, at paragraph 48, concludes that: "The Geneva Conventions enjoy nearly universal participation, as virtually all states are parties to the four Geneva Conventions. It is also generally accepted that most of their provisions are regarded as declaratory as customary international law." And lastly I would point, in terms of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, to the Kupreskic Trial Chamber's decision at paragraphs 519 to 520, where the Court finds, and I quote: "Further, most norms of international humanitarian law, in particular those prohibiting war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, are also peremptory norms of international law or jus cogens; i.e., of a non-derogable and overriding character." The second point relates to when the conventions are applicable from, if you accept the proposition that they're customary international law. The date of independence is March 6th, 1992, and as they're applicable from the date of independence, there is no difficulty in this case, as the indictment starts from May 1992. Even if the Court was to determine that it wasn't until they were recognised as a state, and that's not the Prosecution's position, that's in April 1992, still long before the scope of the time frame of the indictment. I would note when we're speaking about the intention of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be bound, that during the time frame that we're speaking about of the indictment, nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina were bound by the grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions as part of their domestic law in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Delic should have been fully aware that he was committing a violation of the grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions as implemented in Bosnia-Herzegovina by a decree of law on the 11th of April, 1992, when Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted implementing legislation in relation to the former Criminal Code, Penal Code, of the SFRY, which implements the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols. That was noted in the Tadic jurisdiction decision at paragraph 132. And the Appeals Chamber in the Jurisdiction Decisions notes the effect of this decree on April 11th, 1992, and states, and I quote: "Hence, nationals of the former Yugoslavia, as well, at present, those of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were therefore aware, or should have been aware, that they were amenable to the jurisdiction of their national criminal courts in cases of violation of international humanitarian law." I'm sure you're aware of the fact that this was also noted by the Trial Chamber in this case in paragraph 312. And the last point simply is just to follow up on a point that was forwarded by Judge Bennouna, which is the concept of state succession. It wasn't, as appears to be before it in the brief of the appellant in this regard, it wasn't an accession to the treaty; it was a secession, and the deposit of the instrument of succession in the depository state of Switzerland was on the 31st of December, 1992. The result, in the Prosecution's submission, is that the application of the Geneva Conventions takes place on the date of independence. And in support of not only that general principle in terms of the law of state secession, it wasn't in our brief, and I apologise that it wasn't. We addressed in our brief only the issue of the application of customary international law. But since it was raised, there are two decisions, and I have them simply to hand them out. They're very short decisions of trial chambers, but simply for your assistance, Your Honours. I apologise that I didn't have them earlier, both for the Court and for the Defence counsel. I'll just explain them as I go. The first one is in the Kovacevic case. It's of the 12th of May, 1998. It's an order on the Prosecution request for judicial notice. The Prosecution, in a motion, asked for judicial notice of a number of things. Two of them were that Bosnia-Herzegovina seceded to the Geneva Conventions -- sorry, to the Genocide Convention of 1949, with an effective date of 6th of March, 1992, and that it declared its independence from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on March 3, 1992. That's a typographical error. It should be the 6th of March. What is important, in the Prosecution's submission, is not necessarily the fact that there's a request that they seceded to the Genocide Convention, the fact that the Trial Chamber admitted these two facts, paragraphs 3 and 4 of the Prosecutor's request, through the means of judicial notice. They took judicial notice that the depositing of the Genocide Convention by Bosnia-Herzegovina as an instrument of secession had the effective date of March 6th, and that was taken as judicial notice. The other decision, which is in the Kordic case of the 2nd of March, 1999, dealt with the -- one of the issues was command responsibility, in Article 7, which had charged them as superiors, including civilians. As you know, Mr. Kordic was a civilian. In paragraph 12, the Trial Chamber concludes that the principle of individual criminal responsibility of superiors for failure to prevent or repress the crimes committed by subordinates can be considered a part of customary international law. The same conclusion has also been reached by another Trial Chamber in the Blaskic decision. I just bring this out in support of my first proposition that the Geneva Conventions and the components of it are part of international customary law. At the end of paragraph 13, under the quote, it notes in the -- it says: "As noted in the Blaskic decision, both the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina are bound by Additional Protocol 1 in this case as successor states of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which has ratified the Protocol on the 11th of June, 1979." Now, it doesn't state the principle that as a successor state it then has an application that goes back to the point of independence, but it does recognise that it is bound as a result of the deposit of the instrument of succession. Those are essentially the points I wanted to make in response to the submissions on the application of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. A couple of quick things. One, as to the status of the conventions as customary international law, I would first note that the more states that become parties to any international convention, the harder it is to tell whether states accept and follow these conventions, because they're treaties that bind the states or because customary international law requires it. It's a bit of a paradox, and I don't know that the Prosecution has overcome that paradox. Clearly, I think that the Secretary-General's decision, or report, while it is good legislative history as to the Statute of the Tribunal, I'm not sure that it's binding on the Tribunal as to what is customary international law. Mr. Farrell said that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina were bound by the same kinds of provisions as the grave breaches provisions as a matter of domestic law. That's fine. I don't disagree with that. And if the Courts in Sarajevo, the domestic municipal courts, choose to prosecute for violations of domestic law, that's their privilege. International courts don't try people for violations of national law. And if we are going to look to that national law, I think, and this may be relevant to an issue that will probably come up tomorrow, the maximum punishment that can be assessed probably should be gauged against that national law also. If we're going to try violations of domestic law in this Tribunal, this Tribunal should have to apply that domestic law, including the maximum punishments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one second, Mr. Moran, before I let you go on. Because it's not at all what the Prosecutor said. You are building a logic based on a concept that is not right. Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was told to you, and that's repeated in the Tadic case that I have in front of me. So Bosnia-Herzegovina said that some of its Tribunals would be competent for some of the crimes based on the 1949 Geneva Conventions and the additional protocol. This was introduced in its legislation, national legislation. But the fact that this is included in the national law, it does not mean that this is not done in the name of international treaties if the aim of international treaties is to be applied within the states. It's not something theoretical, abstract, so I don't really follow you. International treaties do -- are applied in the states that have signed them, and they are applied when the state in question is party to this treaty, and these treaties are applied, implemented by the tribunals of the states in question. That's what has been told to you. So it's possible that you have a national Tribunal, an International Tribunal that applied the same convention. That's possible. International convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I misunderstood Mr. Farrell, but I thought that one of the things he said was that Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted, as a matter of domestic law, the SFRY Penal Code provisions, which essentially mirror the grave breaches provision as a matter that these defendants should not be surprised that they're bound by the grave breaches provision, because they knew they were bound by domestic law. And my -- and what I was just arguing was not that treaties do not apply within states, but that the argument seemed to have been that you knew that you were bound by domestic law that mirror the grave breaches, and therefore, you should not be surprised at some later date if you are charged with exactly the same thing for violations of the grave breaches. I hope I'm not mangling Mr. Farrell's argument too badly, but I think that was the essence of it. I stand to be corrected, but it seems to be a fair assessment. And if we're going to do that, then I think that you can't take parts of the domestic law. You have to take it all. If you're saying he's not going to be surprised by an issue. But in any case, that's something I was going to talk about later on, tomorrow. It's more relevant to tomorrow. Finally, and I think this is the actual bottom-line position that I take is that pick a date relevant to the indictment, July 1st, 1992. If someone picked up the phone on July 1st, 1992 and called the Swiss council, the Swiss government, and said, "Hey, is Bosnia-Herzegovina a party to the Geneva Conventions? Are they bound by the grave breaches provisions?" The answer from the Swiss government probably would have been no, for the simple reason that the instrument of succession had not been filed and Bosnia-Herzegovina had not joined the conventions at that time. Now, is it fundamentally fair to prosecute an individual for a violation of a law, be it a national law or an international law, which at the time the act was committed, he could not tell was a violation of that law? And I just don't think it is fundamentally fair to do that. And unless there's some other questions from the bench, that's all I have on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr. Moran. You can stay standing, because we move now to group 4 and you are carrying the burden of that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm in the hot seat again. I understand this is the difference between internal and international armed conflict and this one I understand I have a hard row to hoe on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but you did tell us you were not going to be very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No. I promise you I will not be very long. It is a hard row to hoe. And let me just suggest this. We were just told by the Prosecutor that customary international law -- or Common Article 3 is customary international law, and we know that because we were told that by the ICJ in Nicaragua versus the United States. And, in fact, in the Tadic decision, the Appeals Chamber cites that as authoritative. Well, either Nicaragua versus United States is authoritative and binding on this Tribunal or it's not. And my suggestion to you is that it may very well be under the charter, the ICJ is the primary judicial organ of the organisation of the United Nations. Where this Tribunal is an organ of another principal organ, the Security Council. In two cases the Appeals Chamber, in Tadic and Aleksovski, the Appeals Chamber specifically rejected the United States versus Nicaragua test for international and internal armed conflict. In fact, in the Aleksovski decision, the Appeals Chamber just came right out and said that the test used by the Tribunal is, "not as rigorous" as the Nicaragua versus United States test, and that's paragraph 145 of the decision. In Aleksovski, the Appeals Chamber discussed at great length, and there was a concurring opinion from Judge Hunt, which I've read, about precedent, but you never discussed the effect of precedent from cases and decisions outside of the International Tribunal. I would suggest that because the ICJ -- sometime earlier today, I can't remember, maybe it was Judge Hunt, said something about Supreme Courts in various jurisdictions may change their minds. It may not have been you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It wasn't me, but I was going to ask you this question later anyway. Where in the Tadic jurisdiction case did they say they were bound by the ICJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour what they said was was it was authoritative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right. But where do they say this Tribunal was bound by the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That may have been quite deliberate, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I am presenting the issue to you for decision whether you are bound by it. Obviously I had nothing to do with the Tadic case, Your Honours. But the question is: If the International Court of Justice is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, essentially the Supreme Court of the United Nations, can another court that is part of the United Nations system abandon or use different legal tests than those enunciated by the Supreme Court, if you would? And I would suggest that they can't. Where the ICJ has spoken that this is customary law or this is a legal test we will use for a matter, that this Tribunal should follow it, and it should follow it for a whole lot of reasons. (1) the ICJ's position within the charter itself; (2) the value of precedent. Remember that in the Kupreskic Trial Chamber, there was some talk about precedent, and as I recall, the Trial Chamber indicated that it was bound by nothing except the decisions from this Chamber. Now, I may be misreading that, I may be misremembering it, but that's what I recall they said. I don't think that's correct unless we're opening every issue up to relitigation every time. If, for instance, the hostages case and the High Command case do not show us what is customary international law as regards to command responsibility, if that is not binding on the Tribunal, then every time the Prosecutor says "customary international law," or, excuse me, "command responsibility," they bear the burden of coming here and showing you that that is customary international law. I don't think that's what this Court has to do. I think that this Court, on issues like that, is bound by the ICJ, the decisions of the ICJ and the decisions of other courts that are widely accepted saying what is customary international law. Having said that, the Trial Chamber used an improper test to determine what is an international armed conflict. They applied the facts that they found to the wrong legal test. Now, the Appeals Chamber can use the proper legal test. Just having quickly read over the evidence, without going into it in any detail because that's not necessary, I would submit that the evidence shows that the officials of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia read Nicaragua versus United States or at least knew that it existed and limited their involvement in the Bosnia war, at least their public involvement, the involvement that could be pinned to them, to that kind of thing, that kind of area where the United States paid the salaries of the Contra officers. FRY paid the salary of officers in the RS army, that type of thing. And that is something that people are allowed to rely on. Finally, just as almost an afterthought, even if the ICJ's decisions are not binding on this Court, it just seems to be unseemly to have two courts -- and undesirable to have two courts, basically a kilometre from each other or a kilometre and a half from each other, having conflicting decisions on the same issue. And with that, unless there are some questions from the Bench, I'll sit down and let the Prosecutor -- and let the Prosecutor respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Farrell again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just firstly the concept argument that this court is somehow bound by the ICJ. Despite its close proximity, it's obvious that this court and the ICJ have different jurisdictions. The ICJ has jurisdiction over states, and as I'm sure you're aware, by its Statute it actually doesn't have the concept of precedent. It's only -- the judgements in the ICJ are only binding on the state parties. Though the decisions, of course, are persuasive, I would submit that it would be rather odd that the decisions of the ICJ are not strictly binding on themselves but they would be binding on this Court which has a different jurisdiction. Secondly, the Appeals Chamber in Tadic, of the 15th of July, 1999, specifically states, at paragraph 115: "The Appeals Chamber, with respect, does not hold the Nicaragua test to be persuasive." In my submission, clearly the Court was fully aware and alive to the issue of the relevance of ICJ decisions. Thirdly, I would note that His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen, in a dissenting opinion, I would note, on another issue in Kanyabashi, as a member of the Appeals Chamber and as in a case of Nsengiyumva, and I'll spell that N-s-e-n-g-i-y-u-m-v-a, has commented on the differences between the International Court of Justice and the Tribunal, and that counsel obviously use care when they use the jurisprudence of the former, being the International Court of Justice, but equally obviously, those differences do not prohibit resource to that jurisprudence on relevant matters, more particularly having regard to the fact that both institutions are international judicial bodies. This in relation to the fact that reference can be made to it, and, obviously, this Court can draw some persuasive value from it but is not, in the Prosecution's submission, bound. It doesn't appear that my friend is arguing too strenuously, although he takes the position that the effective control test was the correct test in the Tadic and Aleksovski judgements. I don't think I need to point out to you that both of those have been overturned by this Chamber. I would note two things though. The first thing is that there are three general scenarios which are recognised in the Tadic decision for the proof of the existence of international armed conflict. The first is the traditional concept of an international conflict between two or more states. The second is where there is an internal armed conflict but it becomes internationalised when a third state intervenes by sending its troops. The third, as recognised by the Appeals Chamber, is that an internal armed conflict becomes internationalised in the situation where at least one of the participants acts on behalf of a foreign state. It's that third scenario, when it's an organised military group that's acting on behalf of a foreign state that is being challenged here. That's where the claim that the effective control test fits in, and that's the third element or third possibility for proving the existence of armed conflict. That's where the Court has held that you would, in those circumstances, apply the overall control test. I would simply bring to your attention that the Trial Chamber in this case considered all three scenarios. They found that there was, under the first scenario, an international conflict between two or more states up until May 19th, when the apparent though, as found by the Trial Chamber, the facade of the removal of the JNA forces from Bosnia-Herzegovina. As the indictment says from May until October, the Trial Chamber made a finding of fact up until at least May 19th that on the first scenario there was an international conflict because the state of the SFRY was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Secondly, if you look at the findings of fact by the Trial Chamber, they make specific findings of fact that there was an intervention by forces of the JNA after May 19th in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That satisfies the second criteria without ever getting to the overall control test or effective control test. I would note the acknowledgement, the factual acknowledgement in the Delic appeal brief on this issue at paragraph 200, and I note that it is written in the appeal brief: "The appellant also agrees, in general terms, with the Trial Chamber that the VJ troops, at various times and in various places in the conflict aided the VRS with special forces," these are armed forces, "logistics, and even in 1994, air support." So on the admission by counsel for Mr. Delic, he's acknowledged the presence, in my submission, of the VJ troops in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on that test alone, we don't have to go to the third test of overall control. In speaking about the issue of the test for overall control and the fact that he raises the question of the application of test to the facts of this case, two points. The first is that the test applied by the Trial Chamber in this case was equally consistent with the overall control test. Though it didn't use the word "overall control," clearly it was long before that decision came out. It applied the same approach as found by the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision and as found in the Appeals Chamber's decision in Aleksovski. The Appeals Chamber decision in Aleksovski states that the overall control test calls for an assessment of all the elements of control taken as a whole and a determination to be made on that basis as to whether there was the required degree of control. The judgement goes through, interestingly enough, the exact same facts, almost as we found in the Tadic decision. It looks at all the elements of control as is indicated as required in the Aleksovski decision, and it concludes that the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the, in the language it uses, the controlling force behind the VRS, which we know is the Bosnian Serb army, in Bosnia. In that regard, it can't be disputed that the test is at least consistent. The last submission I would make is that the elements and facts as found by the Trial Chamber are almost identical but at least very similar to the facts relied on in the Tadic appeal decision. Now, I'll bring to your attention the original position of the appellants in their appeal brief. They originally said that the facts were similar to Tadic. In fact, in the Landzo appeal brief, counsel used the words that the facts in this case were remarkably similar to the facts in the Tadic case. Of course, that was at a time when the Tadic case applied the effective control test. And their legal argument was that as the effective control test was the correct test and the facts are remarkably similar, you should reach the same result. Well, I'd simply bring to your attention that now the test as found in Tadic on remarkably similar facts came to the conclusion that this Trial Chamber did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, do you want to rely to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're asking the Court to apply the correct legal test, and along those lines, we must recall that everyone agrees that at some points in time, the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina was considered to be internal and at other times external or international. An example is a report given to his government by the -- by a member of the commission of experts where he said that activities in BH prior to April 6, 1992 should be considered as internal, activities between 6 April 1992 and May 1992 should be considered as international, and those after 19 May should be considered as internal. That's on page 102 and paragraph 225 of my brief, and it's quoting out of a book, L.C. Green, "The Contemporary Law of Armed Conflict" in 1996. By the way, it quotes Bill Fenrick. And we just ask the Court to apply the proper legal test to the facts that were found by the Trial Chamber, that the improper test was used and that we would like the proper test used. And having done that, I think you'll find it was an internal armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Don't sit down, because you're going to be first up in relation to group 3, protected persons, because Mr. Ackerman said he did not wish to add to anything that was in his written submissions and what he'd said earlier in relation to Count 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll move down to the podium. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moran, while you're standing, one question about the international aspect of the conflict. My question is the following: You tell us -- to sum up, you're telling us that the Chamber, in this particular case, has not applied the proper legal test that should be the one of Nicaragua, and you tell us that this Tribunal is bound by the ICJ. In Tadic, in the appeal in 1999, I'd like to point to the fact that the Chamber did not move from the Nicaragua test. What they did for the Nicaragua case is that they interpreted it in a different way, and here I would be very much interested in your opinion, because then the Chamber said: [In English] "This criterion will be used in practice," the criterion is the criterion of effective control, "would be used in practice only with regard to individuals or unorganised groups of individuals acting on behalf of the state." [Intepretation] So that's way the Chamber has limited or restricted the Nicaragua test of effective control for groups of individuals, because then this -- the behaviour of these individuals is then put to the credit of a state. [In English] It has applied a different test, that is the test of overall control, with regard to military or paramilitary groups, which the Appeals Chamber termed overall control.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the real question is that in Tadic in 1999, the test of effective control was limited to the actions of individuals and groups of -- disorganised groups of individuals, because then we are -- for attributing the behaviour to a state, whereas when we have paramilitary groups, and that's what we're interested in, then we apply the test of overall control that should be used to attribute the behaviour of these paramilitary groups to a particular state. And then to lead to the internationalisation of the conflict because you would say that a specific state intervenes in another state through a paramilitary group. Do you have this distinction in mind, this difference in mind, in terms of the legal test used to assess the international nature of a conflict? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour, if I'm going to give you a good answer, but I'll give you the best one I can, which is this: The contras in Nicaragua versus United States were a pretty well-organised paramilitary organisation. They were funded when congress decided to fund them, pretty well, they were supported by various organs of the United States government, and they carried on a pretty organised campaign against the elected government of Nicaragua. At a minimum, I think one would have to call them a paramilitary group. The ICJ talked about them having officers and commanders and organisations. I don't think that they should be treated, for purposes of international versus internal armed conflict, different from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to enter into a reanalysis of the Nicaragua and contra case, Mr. Moran. The Appeals Chamber of our Tribunal, International Criminal Tribunal, has criticised the ICJ for the way in which it applied international law in terms of responsibility, and there was a test of responsibility in the Nicaragua case. The Tribunal said that the ICJ had not applied the appropriate test; i.e., that for a paramilitary group, the overall control test is the one which is applicable. We said that the ICJ had applied an erroneous test, one which was not adapted. It was the effective control test, which, according to the Appeals Chamber, only applies to individuals or groups of non-organised individuals. So this is the situation we find ourselves in. The Appeals Chamber has indeed criticised the manner in which the ICJ had implemented customary international law in terms of international liability, so that a paramilitary group now can be said to be linked to a state, thanks to the application of the overall control test, without it being necessary for the state to be responsible for the conduct of this group in any situation. And this, of course, leaves the problem of individual criminal responsibility untouched, as it does with the problem of the command responsibility. So this is the problem that was put. The Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal did criticise the ICJ on this particular issue because it thought that the ICJ had applied an inappropriate test and had applied inappropriately international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Now I understand your question. I did not want to re-fight the contra war, and I'm glad I don't have to. The Appeals Chamber here has taken the position -- I think it is best put in Aleksovski, where it says that the test that should be used, the test that this Appeal Chamber should use, is "not as rigorous" as the ICJ test, and this Tribunal and the Appeals Chamber has been critical of the ICJ. I have no problem with this Chamber being critical of the ICJ. The suggestion that I put before the Court is, and I guess it's more of a question than -- as much as a proposition of law, is whether, on the same issue of law, whether a conflict is an international armed conflict or an internal armed conflict, whether the two courts, as a matter of policy, should have different legal tests; and if not, who prevails? And my submission was that under the Charter, as the primary judicial organ of the United Nations, when it comes to that kind of conflict, that the ICJ should prevail, whether I like what the ICJ holds or not, just because of their position under the Charter. Did I answer your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that on this particular issue, you are assuming that the ICJ should prevail, or its decisions should prevail, on the decisions rendered by the ICTY. But that's not what we're looking at. You see, the idea is that the ICJ has a completely different mission, a completely different competence. There is nothing similar between what the ICTY has to do, what the ICJ has to do. The ICJ does not deal with similar types of problems as we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, but the question is: Can you have two separate rules of law on the same issue from two courts, one applicable to states and one applicable to individuals? I happen to be from a jurisdiction that has two supreme courts. In my state, unlike virtually every other state in the United States, we have a Supreme Court that does civil cases and a court of criminal appeals that does nothing but criminal cases. They will sometimes interpret the same Statute, and they do everything they can to make sure that they interpret it the same way. And when they don't, and I think there have been two or three occasions when they have not, the second court to decide is usually pretty well criticised, and they're criticised for not having a consistent body of jurisprudence. And I would suggest that that is not too different from the situation between the ICJ and the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Surely, Mr. Moran, that is because each of them stands at the pinnacle of the appellate procedures in that particular state, so that the courts below them would be somewhat confused if they had two appellate courts telling them different things about the same Statute. That's not the situation here at all. We do not bind anybody else by our decisions, except the Trial Chamber's, and the ICJ doesn't bind anybody, doesn't even bind itself by its decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I understand it, the ICJ generally, although they say that the Statute says it's not precedential, as we would have in the common-law world, they do, when they find that something is customary international law, they tend to keep applying that standard. And while you say that no one else is bound by the holdings of this Court, or the ICJ, for that matter, except the states involved or the Trial Chambers here, the fact of the matter is that people and states are bound by the decisions of this Court; people and states are bound by the holdings of the ICJ; that somewhere in most countries where there is a military, there are people in uniforms, lawyers, who are reading the decisions from this trial, from this Court, and determining what constitutes customary international law, what do we have to do to follow international law, what does the Geneva Convention mean, those kinds of issues. This Court stands in a very similar situation to the Control Counsel 10 cases to the courts or the Nuremberg Tribunal. You are enunciating international law, just as there is someone in a foreign ministry someplace who is reading the decisions of the ICJ, saying, "Here's what our government can do or cannot do." They pay lawyers lots of money to do that. And "Here is what is customary international law binding upon our state." And when those two groups of lawyers get together, they ought to have the same law. There should not be one set of customary international law binding individuals and another set of customary international law applying to states. It should be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moran, I think maybe we should swiftly go on to the next point, because we are now hearing you launch an analysis or a transposition of international law which might lead us way beyond what we are gathered here to discuss. I'm speaking under the control of Judge Hunt, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And I understand, and I will defer to Judge Hunt's request to go on, the request made through you, Your Honour. The next thing up is the effect of nationality on protected persons, and we're going to break this into two areas basically. The first thing I'm going to do is talk about the Trial Chamber's holdings, this Appeals Chamber's holdings in Tadic and Aleksovski, and treaty interpretation. And then Mr. Karabdic is going to talk about the citizenship law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the simple reason that he knows it a lot better than I do. Part of the element of the offence for a violation, a grave breach of the Geneva Convention relative to civilians, is that that person be a protected person within the definition of Article 4 of the Convention. It's a treaty interpretation case. It's pretty well settled, at least by the ICJ, that when you're interpreting a treaty, a court should interpret the words according to their natural and ordinary meanings in the context in which they occur. And the case cite on that, the cite in my brief, is Cambodia versus Thailand. It's a 1961 case. When we're interpreting treaties, when courts interpret treaties, they're not writing treaties; they're interpreting agreements that have been made by sovereign states, where sovereign states have agreed to be bound by certain provisions of these treaties. I think if you look at the plain wording of a treaty and it says something, it shouldn't be broadened, it shouldn't be narrowed. The agreement of the parties should be followed. Now, having said that, there are two cases from the Appeals Chamber, obviously, Tadic and Aleksovski, that I want to talk about, because I have to -- because they set a test for what is a protected person. Yesterday we were discussing a matter having to do with knowledge, and somebody said, "Is this an academic exercise?" Well, in Tadic and Aleksovski, given the facts that were found by the Trial Chambers and this Chamber, any discussion on nationality and protected persons was an academic exercise. It was dicta. It was not necessary to the decision of the Appeals Chamber. And here's why: In both of those cases, the Trial Chamber -- or the Appeals Chamber, rather, held that given the facts of the case, there was, one, an international armed conflict, in one case involving the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the other, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it further held that the, in one case Bosnian Serbs, the other case Croatian, Bosnian Croatians, were agents of the other power; in one case FRY and the other case Croatia. So that citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Croats, were in the hands of a party to the conflict of which they were not nationals, Croatia or FRY. Then the Court went on to hold that when we look at the definition of protected persons and we talk about nationals of a country, that in this era the proper thing to do is to look at which side of the conflict that a party is on or identified with, so that, for instance, a Bosnian Muslim who is in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs would be a protected person. That is what I consider to be dicta, because it is unnecessary for the decision of the case. Now, if it's not dicta, if it's binding on you, I would suggest that it's wrongly decided and that you should consider revisiting those issues, and here are the reasons. As we said earlier, the general rule of treaty interpretation is one interprets the words of the treaty, and Article 4 of Geneva Convention talks about protected persons being those who are in the hands of a party to the conflict of which they are not nationals. It doesn't say anything about being identified with one side of a conflict or another; it says what it says. As Mr. Karabdic will show you in a few minutes, or at least attempt to show you, based on the evidence that was presented by experts and evidence that was presented at the trial level, everybody involved in this case was a national of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at all relevant times to this conflict. The inmates in the prison were residents of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the people holding -- or were, excuse me, nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not just residents. The people who were the guards were nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they were part of the army, or the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, part of the normal governmental function of that republic. Now, when you examine the history of the Geneva Convention relative to civilians, you have to do a couple of things, I think. Remembering that it was passed in -- or it was adopted by the Diplomatic Convention in 1949 and then ratified by various states over a period of years.
