The Pictet's commentaries to the convention talk about the definition of protected persons being in a negative form so as to -- they're intended to cover anyone who's not a national, but not interfere with the relations of a state with its own nationals. A couple of courts have construed other portions of the conventions, or of the other conventions. Two that I cited involved the construction of the convention on prisoners of war, Koi and Lee Hoo Boon, both of which involved people who claimed prisoner of war status when they were being held by the state of which they were nationals. In both cases, one, the privy counsel, House of Lords acting as privy counsel, and the other the Malaysia Supreme Court, held that no, they were not in the hands of the enemy. They were not protected under customary law. And we discussed these at some length in our brief. It is general international law, in my opinion and my submission to the Court, that international law does not get involved or interfere with a state's relations with its own nationals, short of genocide and crimes against humanity. The highest protection any individual can have under international law is that of a diplomat, and yet the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations excludes diplomats credited to their own state, if you would. And with the help of the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is an hour and a half since we started. We'll take a break now until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please, the Court, Your Honour. As I was saying before the break, the highest protection under international law given to any individual is that to diplomatic agents under the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations. The general rule is that a diplomat can do anything he wants, commit any crime he wants in the nation to which he's accredited, and he cannot be tried for an allegation unless his own state waives immunity. There is one exception to that, and that exception is for diplomats who are nationals of the state to which they are accredited. That's Article 38(1) of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. During the break we handed out a news magazine article to show how that works. It's the top article. Basically it talks about the Ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the United Nations, who was arrested in New Orleans, Louisiana for cheating in a casino. He claimed diplomatic immunity, and at first blush, the United Nations people that were in charge of that agreed that he had diplomatic immunity, and later called back and said that no, they were wrong. Because he's a United States national, he does not have diplomatic immunity vis-a-vis the United States except for his official position. Now, if nationality, citizenship in a state is the determining factor on whether or not one has diplomatic immunity, clearly it can be a determining factor on whether or not a person is a protected person under the definition in Article 4 of the Geneva Convention relative to civilians. The basic holding of the Trial Chamber and the dicta in Tadic and Aleksovski seems to be that given the change in how wars are fought, the 1949 conventions may be obsolete and may need to be updated to take into account a so-called new reality. Maybe that's true. I'm not going to disagree, as a matter of public policy, that possibly the conventions are obsolete. If they are, maybe we should convene a new diplomatic conference in Geneva, just like was convened in 1949, and look at rewriting or replacing the conventions, possibly passing Protocols 3 and 4, if that's required, and at that point, the states of the world can determine whether they want to ratify and be bound by the new conventions and the new holdings. But if those conventions are to be rewritten, if protections under those conventions to be extended to people that are not protected by the plain language of the 1949 conventions, I know it's not my job to do that, and I don't think it's the job of the Prosecutor, and I don't think it's the job of the Security Council. It's the right of states, through negotiations, to arrive at major changes in the Geneva Conventions. By their very nature, international conventions are the subject of negotiation among multiple state parties, and they're the result of compromise by those parties. There's no question in my mind that the Tribunal has the power to construe the Geneva Conventions pretty much anyway the Tribunal so chooses. The question in my mind is: Should it do so or should apply the traditional rules of treaty interpretation to read the plain language of the treaty as ratified by virtually every state in the world, with the possible exception of Burma, and apply that treaty as it's written or should the Tribunal decide that the treaty is obsolete and should be rewritten? I think it should do the former, apply the traditional rules. The evidence in this case has been all along, from the witnesses that testified, that they testified in such a way to show that they were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nobody ever tried to give up that citizenship, renounce it, accept citizenship in another state. They were all residents of Bosnia-Herzegovina, most of them from the time of their birth. We introduced evidence that they had been born there, educated there, married there, voted there. They had all the indicia -- they lived there. They had all the indicia of citizenship. If we're going to start giving citizens rights and liabilities and dividing citizens up under the law based on their ethnicity, I would suggest that that is an awfully slippery slope, that my country has a history of doing that, and whenever we've done it we've been, in the long run, very sorry. Just over a little over 24 hours ago, the United States, in a case called Saldano versus Texas -- and I will provide a copy to the Court, I only have one copy -- vacated a death sentence because the Prosecution, at the punishment phase, presented evidence that Mr. Saldano, who is an Argentinian national, was more likely to commit future crimes because his Hispanic background. Now, I'm his lawyer, and I found that offensive. I found it very offensive that his ethnic background would have anything to do with his status under the law, and the Supreme Court agreed with me. Your Honour, unless there are some questions about what I've talked about, I'll sit down and let Mr. Karabdic tell you about what the Bosnian citizenship law was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karabdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo. I am going to address the topic of the BiH citizenship. In paragraph 225 of the judgement, it is said that the analysis of the citizenship of the BiH is not fully clear. Also, in paragraph 252, it says that even though Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed its independence in March 1992, it was only in October 1992 that the first decision regulating the issue of citizenship was passed and which was later supplemented with others. I have to say that these -- that the Trial Chamber has erred in its ruling, and the citizenship of Bosnia and Herzegovina was, as a result, misinterpreted, especially in its application of Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions Relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War, and it was prejudicial to my client. Such judgement would not have been possible had the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina been treated as citizenship of an independent sovereign state. Bosnia and Herzegovina was immediately recognised as a sovereign state and became a state among the other internationally recognised states. Further, in paragraph 168 of the Tadic appeal, the Appeal Chamber allows for a possibility that prior to 6 October 1992, when the law of the citizenship of BiH was passed, that the citizens of FRY had the same rights as the BiH citizens. Now, that too is not true. The analysis of this issue needs to start with the constitutions of SFRY and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the constitution of the federal state and its constituent republics, which were then socialist. The constitution of 1974 says that SFRY is a federal state, a union of its constituent republics. The constitution of the Socialist Republic of BiH states that BiH is a sovereign state of its constituent people, including Serbs, Croats, Muslims and other groups who live there. The citizens of Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina exercised their rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and also in the SFRY, when it is in their interest. This same applies for the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, and members of other ethnic groups, shall exercise their rights in Bosnia-Herzegovina, except for their rights which are of common interest, for which it is provided that they should be exercised within the SFRY. SFRY, pursuant to the constitution of 1974, was a federal state with many elements of confederation. Some of this also applies to the issue of citizenship. There was a citizenship of the federal state, that is, SFRY, and the citizenship of individual republics, such as SR BiH. Every citizen of any of its constituent republics was simultaneously a citizen of SFRY. This is paragraph 249.2. And also it is reflected in the -- Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution has the same provision. There were two laws: the law of citizenship of SFRY adopted in 1976 and the law of citizenship of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted in 1977. Both laws had almost identical legal and material provisions. Only the SFRY citizenship law provided for the annulment of citizenship. It also contained colliding provisions. In both of these laws, the SFRY and the BiH laws, all issues relating to the citizenship was left to the republican organs, and it was the republican organs which would register its citizens. Until the proclamation of independence, the BiH citizens held two citizenships: one SFRY and the other SR BiH. The primary citizenship was the BiH citizenship, whereas the SFRY was derived -- it could not exist on its own -- it was just derived from the republican citizenship. This was the situation until the beginning of the war. A referendum was held on 29 February and 1 March of 1992, and two thirds of those who came out to vote voted for independence. The independence was proclaimed on 6 March 1992, and Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina became Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, the new state was immediately attacked and the war broke out. By the recognition of its independence, the citizenship of SR BiH became the citizenship of the Independent Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was no longer part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And so citizenship of SFRY could not be derived from the BiH citizenship. The law of SR BiH was fully adopted by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in the first days of its independence the citizenship of BiH was fully regulated. The presidency of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted a decree with a force of law of 11 April 1992, adopting the laws of the previous state as new republican laws, and through this decree, over 200 federal laws were adopted and were put into force as the republican laws, including the law on citizenship with the necessary changes. According to the constitution of Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the presidency of the republic, in case of the immediate threat of war and inability to convene the parliament, had the right it adopt decrees with the force of law. Later on, the decree with the force of law of SR BiH were further clarified. It was adopted in October 1992 and it represents only the codification of the previous regulations rather than a belated regulating of the issue of the citizenship of BiH as was found by the Trial Chamber. According to paragraph 252 of the Trial Chamber's judgement, all citizens of BiH were also citizens of the SFRY until this state was dissolved. Dr. Gow, who was a Prosecution expert, presented his views on this issue and said that the SFRY was dissolved in April 1992, at the latest, and ceased to exist as a state. On 27 April 1992, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed with its new -- and the new constitution was adopted, and formally this is the moment when all Yugoslavia ceased to exist. Based on this -- with these new laws, the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina can no longer be treated as citizens of this new state. Provisions were also made for citizens in succession when a state ceased to exist. The citizens can only get the citizenship of the successor state. Professor Economides, another Prosecution expert witness, testified to that. The citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including those of Serbian ethnic origin, had only one citizenship as of April 1992, which was the citizenship of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina of Serb ethnic background could not become citizens of the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia because the citizenship of the new state was limited only to people living in its constituent parts, which was the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro, and the reference are paragraphs 17 and 21. The Trial Chamber further says even though the Badinter Commission, states successor states must allow a possibility for its citizens to opt for other citizenships, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia never exercised this right. I have to make a point here that the Badinter Commission never provided for the minority groups to exercise the right but only recommended it. It said it would be very appropriate. The BH citizen law does not provide a possibility for its citizens of Serb ethnic background to opt for a Federal Republic of Yugoslavia citizenship, and it requires that the state of whose citizenship an applicant may apply for has to first provide proof of the approval of this state to grant such a request, which is not the case. Dayton Accords further provides that all citizens living in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina are granted the citizenship of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the citizens naturalised after 6th of April 1992 shall be regulated subsequently. The Dayton Accord, therefore, makes it clear that the citizenship of Bosnia and Herzegovina existed as early as 6th of April, 1992. These are my submissions, and if there are any questions, I'm open to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karabdic, for the all the information you have forwarded to us. It has been an extremely interesting introduction to practices that you know, because you come from the inside of the system and you have told us a lot about the evolution of the concept of nationality since the existence of the Federal Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the SFRY. I have a question that relates to Article 4 of the Geneva Convention, an Article which implies that -- maybe my question also goes to Mr. Moran, who also spoke at length on this particular issue, Article 4, which defines what is a protected person. What I am interested in is the situations in which this Article applies. They apply normally in cases of international conflict. If we assume that the conflict of an international character, the victims must also be proven to be protected persons as defined by Article 4 of the Geneva Convention. This Article 4, I have it before me in English, and it says, I quote: [In English] "At a given moment and in any manner whatsoever, find themselves in case of a conflict or occupation in the hands of a party to the conflict." "Find themselves in the hands of a party to the conflict." [Interpretation] So this is where the notion of protected persons arises from. These persons are individuals who, at a particular moment in time, find themselves in between the hands of one of the parties who are at war. And the text adds, "Or of an occupying power, [In English] they are not nationals." [Interpretation] That means they are not citizens of that particular country. So we are speaking of individuals who are in between the hands of a belligerent party and a party of which they are not a citizen. Mr. Moran told us that this text, sorry, should be read in the light of what it actually says, that only the words matter here. We have to look at the words as they have been written. In the Tadic case, it was added by Mr. Moran that the Vienna Convention was quoted, that what was to be looked at was the natural meaning of the words, but what was also to be taken into account was the more general aim of the treaty. So this is what one calls theological interpretation. If we try to look, as you said, Mr. Moran, at the meaning of the words and the words only, we notice that the persons who find themselves in between the hands of a state of which they are not a citizen, in a situation where there is a conflict between two states, then it is quite clearly persons who have the nationality of the enemy state. So the question I have is the following: What about a conflict such as the one that we are discussing here, a conflict that has taken place in Bosnia which is qualified as being an international conflict? It's an internal conflict that has become internationalised, and this conflict involves Bosnia and Herzegovina and another party in this internationalised conflict. In that case, the Bosnian Serbs, who it may appear may have the same formal nationality as the Muslim Bosnians but who are, in fact, individuals who belong to the other party in the conflict. So in such a situation, how does the Article 4 of the Geneva Convention apply? How does it apply? Really, this is what interests me. The interpretation which was given to us beforehand was that this convention, contrary to what Mr. Moran has said, this 1949 convention, as all international conventions, has a life of its own and an evolution of its own. This was the decision made by the Appeals Chamber of our Tribunal. And it appears that some conventions have even been enriched by the behaviour of the parties of the conventions, behaviours that have a customary law value, so to speak. We are speaking of a text that was written in 1949. It is well understood that from 1949 to 1992 things have developed and changed, a lot of time has gone by, so that this Article has to be interpreted bearing in mind the general aim of the convention and not in the context of the way conflicts have developed, because these conflicts, more and more, are interethnic conflicts, and I am speaking here of conflicts in the former Yugoslavia. In those cases, foreign states are not involved. We are speaking of conflicts between different ethnicities. So this is the situation in which we find ourselves. What can you answer to that question, Mr. Moran, Mr. Karabdic? Whoever wishes to speak is welcome to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'd like to speak to that if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll let Mr. Moran answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the convention is agreement among states. Absent the agreement among states to the terms of this convention, nothing exists. I've provided the Trial Chamber and this Chamber with various authorities from some governments on their interpretations of Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions. The one that comes to mind is the one produced by the US Judge Advocate General School, their law of war desk book from 1997. They all agree, everything I've seen from a government, agrees that when the convention says "in the hands to the party of a conflict of which he is not a national," it means being in the hands of a party to a conflict of which he is not a national. As I said, it's possible that the Geneva Conventions are obsolete. In 1949, there was a diplomatic conference to rewrite the 1920 Geneva Conventions in light of the experience of World War II, and they produced what we have today. It is possible that we need a 2001 diplomatic meeting to write conventions for the world as it exists in this new millennium. However, until that is done, we are faced with a law, a treaty, that is written in very specific terms, aimed at very specific things, protecting very specific types of people. And what we have is a situation where in an international armed conflict -- remember, Your Honour, that in an internal armed conflict, with the exception of Common Article 3, nothing applies from the Geneva Convention. You're talking about a conflict which has been internationalised; that is, a foreign state has taken part, taken over, has control over one side of a conflict within the borders of the sovereign State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a state that has all the rights of my state, your state, everybody else's state. People -- the question then becomes: How much protection does international law give to persons who are citizens of a state within that state, owing loyalty to that state, who take part in an international armed conflict on the other side? I think we can all agree that's the bottom line. In this day and age, under the law as it is written today, those people have the protections of their national law. They have the rights that are given to them under their constitution to fair trials and whatever else they have. There is a question, and we've discussed it and it's not -- I don't know whether it's relevant here or not, on the application of Common Article 3 to international armed conflict, because it's clearly -- by its very terms only applies to internal. If it's applicable, then they would have the protections of Common Article 3. They would not be protected from their own state by the IV Geneva Convention. There would be some protection, in an international armed conflict, to the entire population, regardless of their nationality and citizenship. That would be part II of the convention. Judge, it's just -- I think the bottom line is we're faced with a law, and it's not the prerogative of anyone, I think, in this room to change that law, that convention. It's open to criticism, and I'll stand here and criticise it with you. But as a matter of law, that clearly-written document should be applied by its own terms. It's unambiguous in its terms, it does not lead to an absurd result to apply its unambiguous words, it clearly reflects the intent of the parties to the convention, and it clearly reflects the intent of the parties who ratified that convention. Your Honour, have I answered your question to your satisfaction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think you have. Without going back to what you have said in your former presentation, I would like to put to you this question: How do you apply the concept of a protected person in the context where you have a conflict that has been internationalised, a conflict that is of an international character and in which both parties, in essence, are members of the same state and yet they are enemies, and they want to protect the civilians of the opposite party? Does that mean that these civilians who find themselves in this international conflict do not benefit from the protection allowed to them by international law?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they have protections. They're protections that apply to all persons in all states for crimes against humanity and genocide. It doesn't make any difference the nationality of the victim of the genocide or crimes against humanity. When German Jews were murdered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Sorry. We are talking about grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions. That is all we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they have no protections under the words of the treaty as it is written. Now, they can -- what they can do is cease to be a citizen or a national of the state that they're in, through whatever procedures there are. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you've just been talking to us previously about the supremacy of the International Court of Justice decisions, and perhaps you are acquainted with the Nottebohm case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you have said the only outlet is that they should be citizens of another country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Or stateless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Or stateless. All right. Now, in fact, Mr. Karabdic mentioned that until after the proclamation of independence, the SFRY nationality could not be derived from the BiH citizenship. Now, this is the official nationality. Now, if you know, according to the Nottebohm case, there is the notion of genuine link. Now, these people, if they are kept to the genuine link with the SFRY, which was designed by the International Court of Justice, the said elements, including some of these elements were the -- I think they mentioned the emotional allegiance, the sense of belonging. So could you -- could you just submit it to your imagination; could you consider that although the nationality of the SFRY could not be derived anymore from the nationality of BiH, it could exist, in fact, on the basis of the general link, and in that case they are still -- they are not citizens of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour Your Honours, the expert witness for the Prosecution witnesses testified that after April -- I keep wanting to say 29th, and I think it's 27th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm just mentioning to you -- I'm just returning your argument that the decisions of the International Court of Justice should be supreme.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. After the founding of the FRY in April of 1992, the -- everyone agrees that the SFRY ceased to exist. When the SFRY ceased to exist, its nationality ceased to exist with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There was another state called Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was another state called the Federal Republic of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And this is the genuine link?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what is a genuine link? I mean, the Court talks about a lot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's what I'm just submitting to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would submit to you that if someone is born in a state, lives in a state, votes in a state, is educated in that state, is married in that state and is physically present within that state, and his relatives were born within that state, died within that state, were educated within that state, and those that are still alive are physically present within the state, that's genuine links, by anybody's standards. And also, the Nottebohm case, recall, Your Honour, had to do with whether Guatemala -- I believe it was Guatemala -- could -- excuse me -- Leichtenstein could exercise its diplomatic protection vis-a-vis Guatemala. And what the Court held was: No, Nottebohm citizenship was basically a fraud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It's the essence, the notion of genuine link.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But what the Court did not rule on is: Could Leichtenstein exercise its sovereignty over Nottebohm? And I submit to you that it could have, that it had the authority to do so. In any case, every -- and if you look at the documents that we introduced in evidence as to each one of the persons named in the indictment and each one of the witnesses for the Prosecution, and the numbers are in my brief somewhere, we have their birth certificates, their voter registration certificates, their marriage certificates, their citizenship certificates, and they all testified that they were living there. Nobody testified they wanted to be -- that they tried to somehow divest themselves of Bosnian nationality, they had taken any official action. They testified fairly consistently that although they didn't vote in the early 1992 referendum, they could have if they had wanted to. They had the option of doing that. With all of those factors, clearly Bosnia-Herzegovina had the right to confer its nationality on those people when it became an independent state in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I understood the thrust of your argument, and it's very powerful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will actually try and be as concise as possible, in light of the time. There's one matter that the Prosecution would like to raise at the beginning, not to take away from anything stated by my learned colleagues but just to state that to the extent that some of the references to laws in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the expression of explanation of what the laws are and how they're brought into effect and what implication they have in Bosnia-Herzegovina, some of that evidence, as far as I'm aware, and I stand to be corrected, was not in evidence. As I understand the reference to the law of the citizenship of the SFRY in 1976, reference to the law of the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1977, presidential decree dated the 11th of April, 1992, adopting over 200 laws, it's my understanding that these aren't in evidence, and I just bring it to your attention that the Prosecution, at least, will attempt to limit its submissions with respect to the findings of the Trial Chamber and the findings of fact, not the evidence before the Trial Chamber. That's my understanding. I may be incorrect. If I can just make a few points immediately about the -- not the issue that was just discussed now, but the first issue, which is: Has this issue been decided? And it's my respectful submission that though it's been an interesting debate, I think the debate, in fact, by my learned colleague on the Defence side is more of the academic one. This matter has been decided by the Appeals Chamber in both Tadic and Aleksovski. The explanation given, at least one of them, by my learned colleague as to why it should be revisited at this stage is that it was not necessary to decide the matter in those cases. As sort of an obiter dictum type of approach, a common-law approach, that you're only bound by the ratio or the decision as it stands in relation to the facts in that case. Accepting that that's the case, accepting that that's the position, I would state just two propositions in that regard. When the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision itself had to deal with two matters which were -- excuse me. If I may, Your Honour, Judge Riad, I'd just ask that if you -- thank you. My apologies. I'm just having a hard time hearing myself, because I speak aloud when I think. Thank you. The first point is that the Tadic Appeals Chamber's decision made particular legal determinations with respect to issues that were before it which did not affect the verdict. That was the determination. For example, one of the issues related to the Trial Chamber's findings on--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Farrell please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: -- purely personal motives. I'm sorry. The Appeals Chamber noted that this finding did not affect the verdict, but concluded that it was a matter of general significance for the Tribunal's jurisprudence and therefore set forth its views. I find it hard to say that the Prosecution could argue that that's an erroneous or a wrong interpretation of the law and that we're in no way bound to at least apply that law in the lower courts in our prosecutions simply because it wasn't specifically a matter that needed to be addressed. Secondly, the -- and the second point I wanted to make was at paragraph 168 of the Tadic decision, in fact the issue was addressed, and it was addressed specifically because of the potential proposition that the October 6, 1992 Citizenship Act in Bosnia-Herzegovina may have resulted in the nationals of the FRY having the same nationality as the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Whether that was the case or not in fact is not the issue. The issue is that this was a potentiality that the Court felt was something that they were required to speak about in case it might be argued that that was the case. So regardless of my friend's argument that because the victims found themselves, in effect, in the hands of the FRY, by being in the hands of the VRS, which were under their overall control, they put forward the proposition that it might be argued that, in fact, they're both citizens -- they're all the same citizens, and that the FRY citizens and Bosnia-Herzegovina citizens were citizens underneath the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That being the case, then there would be no difference in citizenship, because they would all be under the SFRY. The Court dealt with that and dealt with the possibility that we face today, which was in Celebici, which is: What do you do in those circumstances? And that's the circumstance we have today. And in my submission, the Court addressed the issue, and specifically addressed it. As the Court held in Aleksovski, before this Appeals Chamber should redetermine a matter, they should look to see whether or not there are cogent reasons. The decision in Aleksovski specifically took careful consideration of the decisions in Tadic and adopted them. I hesitate to say that the Appeals Chamber in Aleksovski -- I hesitate that the submission could be made, and I'm not making it, that the Appeals Chamber in Aleksovski didn't consider the matter very clearly but simply adopted it because it was said by an Appeals Chamber previously. In fact, in relation to the international armed conflict, from which the protected persons issue flowed, the Court in Aleksovski said that they gave careful consideration to it. For those reasons, there are no cogent reasons for this matter to be revisited and that this Court is bound. Just to make a couple of points, if I may, with respect to the comments on treaty interpretation. The Vienna Convention, in the language, says that the treaty is to be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning, but that ordinary meaning is clarified as that meaning to be given in the terms of the treaty in their context and in light of their object and purpose. You just don't simply read the word, and because it is a word that you can understand and is something that seems to make sense based on the normal interpretation, that that, in and of itself, is the end of the interpretation of the word. In fact, it seems that the more logical approach would be that it's the starting point, it's the prima facie guide, and this rule of interpretation cannot be allowed to obstruct the essential quest in the application of treaties, namely, to search for the real intention of the contracting parties. Now, as Tadic held in the Appeals Chamber decision, in looking at the decision itself, it looked at -- the Geneva Conventions since 1949, it looked at the legal bond of nationality. And in the decision, at paragraph 165, it said that the legal bond of nationality was not regarded in 1949 as crucial. When we're looking at the interpretation of the Geneva Conventions today, it's not that we're changing the law, as my learned colleague has said, and we're trying to apply a different law. The Court noted, the Appeals Chamber noted in Tadic, that there was allowance made in the Geneva Conventions for special cases, for example, stateless persons. It also spoke about civilians in occupied territory. Clearly, civilians in occupied territory have the nationality of the party in which they are in the hands of, and the example was the German Jew refugees in France. So clearly there wasn't an intention to determine that nationality was the sole criteria. When you look at the Tadic decision as well, there is, in addition to as I've just mentioned, there's also recognition of the types of conflict that the law operates within, and in my submission this is relevant to the terms of the treaty and their interpretation and the fact it is to be read in the context in which the treaty was made, which is that it made special allowance for these types of circumstances. It also, as has been expressed by Judge Bennouna, that you might take a more teleological approach, which is to interpret based on the function of the treaty. And in this case, the function, as indicated by Tadic, which is the true object and purpose is the protection of civilians to the maximum extent. And it would be my submission that to adopt some type of interpretation as advocated by my learned colleague, in situations where you would have an international armed conflict, where you would have the prima facie application of the Geneva Conventions, where you would have citizens who have allegiance to a foreign state, where you have a breakdown of the state so it's not clear how the state is composed, and where you have those citizens detained as the civilian enemy, but then you don't apply the Geneva Convention because you don't apply an approach which attempts to abide by the object and purpose of that very convention, in my submission, that would be illogical and would actually result in the removal of protections from the Geneva Convention, contrary to its very object and purpose. Subject to any questions, those are my submissions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I know you said nothing in chief, as it were, but you do have the right of reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have nothing, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Moran?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can be very quick about it, and with that, I'll sit down. But quickly going over this, treaty interpretations. The words of the treaty are the prima facie guide. The words of the treaty are the treaty. That is the intent of the parties to the treaty, what they wrote down, what they wrote there. The Prosecution says that "How about citizens of occupied territories," and uses the example of the German Jews. That's real easy to take care of. The authors of the convention took that into consideration, and there's a special provision -- and I want to say that it's Article 68, but just as sure as I say that, it will be some other article -- that provides that a refugee who left his state prior to the outbreak of the conflict has a special status under the convention, that the authors took that into consideration. Whether this court should revisit it, revisit Tadic and Aleksovski. The first thing I would say is that this Appeals Chamber has, in fact, overruled its own precedent in the past when it thought it was wrong, and that was in the Tadic sentencing appeal, where this Appeals Chamber overruled Erdemovic without even bothering to cite it. Your Honours, I suggest that the treaty should be interpreted as pursuant to the intent of the parties that entered into it. If it's obsolete, this Court can say so and can call for a new convention. And that, Your Honours, is all I have on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: at 5.31 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday the 7th day of June, 2000, at 10 a.m.
